children.translated_text: In the northern direction there exists, divine in nature,
a king of mountains named <s>Himālaya</s>,
plunging into the eastern and western oceans,
standing like a measuring rod of the earth.
Regarding whom all mountains, treating [him] as a calf,
with <s>Meru</s> standing as the milker skilled in milking,
milked forth radiant gems and great herbs
from the earth, taught [to be milked] by <s>Pṛthu</s>.
Of that [mountain], the source of endless gems,
the snow has not diminished [his] splendor;
for a single defect, amid an assembly of virtues,
sinks away, like the dark spot in the rays of the moon.
And he who bears upon his peaks
the provider of ornaments for the playful sports of <s>Apsarases</s> —
with colors distributed by the gaps in the clouds,
intoxicated with mineral pigments, like an untimely twilight.
The clouds moving up to [his] girdle-zone —
seeking the shade that clings to the lower slopes,
disturbed by the rains, <s>Siddhas</s> (perfected beings) resort to
his peaks, which are sunny.
The <s>Kirātas</s> (tribal hunters), seeing the footsteps, reddened but washed clean by streams of snow,
even without seeing the [actual] slain elephants,
know the path of lions on him
by the pearls released from the cavities of [their] claws.
Where birch-bark sheets, red as elephant-drops,
inscribed with letters in mineral pigment,
serve the purpose of the beautiful women of the <s>Vidyādharas</s>
for composing love letters to <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless god of love).
He who, filling the hollows of bamboo reeds
with wind issuing from the mouths of caves,
seems to wish to assume the role of a drone-provider
for the <s>Kiṃnaras</s> (celestial musicians) about to sing.
Where the fragrance from <s>sarala</s> (pine) trees,
rubbed by elephants to relieve the itching of their cheeks,
exuding like flowing milk,
perfumes the slopes.
Where, for the forest-dwelling [couples] accompanied by their wives,
the luminous herbs, whose radiance clings to the interiors of their cave-dwellings,
become at night
lamps for lovemaking that require no oil.
Where, although the path has ice hardened into stone, irritating the tips of toes and heels,
even upon such a path,
the <s>Aśvamukhī</s> (horse-faced celestial women), burdened by heavy hips and breasts,
do not break their slow gait.
He who shelters in his caves from the sun
the darkness that lurks there by day, as if frightened;
surely, even toward a humble one who has sought refuge,
the lofty-minded feel a sense of protectiveness.
With their splendid tails waving and spreading here and there,
white as moonbeams,
the <s>Camarī</s> (yak-cows) with their tail-fans make meaningful
the title 'king of mountains' for him.
Where, for the <s>Kiṃpuruṣa</s> women embarrassed by the displacement of garments,
by chance,
the clouds, with reflections hanging at the doors of cave-dwellings,
become curtains.
The wind that bears the spray of the <s>Bhāgīrathī</s>'s (Ganges') cascades,
repeatedly shaking the <s>devadāru</s> (deodar) cedars,
is enjoyed by <s>Kirātas</s> tracking deer,
[the wind] that has torn apart the peacocks' tail-feathers.
The sun, revolving below,
leaving behind [only] those lotuses from which the Seven Sages have gathered [the rest],
with upward-directed rays, awakens
the lotuses at the tips of his summit-lakes.
Considering his being the source of sacrificial ingredients,
and his essential capacity to bear the earth,
<s>Prajāpati</s> himself bestowed upon him
the lordship over mountains, with an appointed share in sacrifices.
He, the friend of <s>Meru</s>, knowing propriety,
for the continuity of his lineage, [married] a daughter of the <s>Pitṛs</s> (ancestors), born of [their] mind —
<s>Menā</s>, worthy of honor even by sages,
befitting himself, he married with due rites.
Then, in the course of time, when between those two
the occasion of lovemaking, befitting their forms, proceeded,
while she bore her delightful youth,
a pregnancy came to be for the wife of the king of mountains.
She gave birth to <s>Mainākā</s>, to be enjoyed by <s>Nāga</s> women,
who had formed a friendship with the ocean;
even when <s>Indra</s> (<s>Vṛtraśatru</s>), the cutter of wings, was enraged,
[Mainākā] knew nothing of the pain of those struck by the thunderbolt.
Then, impelled by the insult of her father
<s>Dakṣa</s>, his daughter, the former wife of <s>Bhava</s> (<s>Śiva</s>),
<s>Satī</s>, the virtuous one, having abandoned her body through <s>yoga</s>,
approached that mountain-bride for [re]birth.
She, auspicious, was born to the lord of mountains,
in that [wife] who was absorbed in meditation —
like prosperity [arising] in a well-executed policy, unimpaired,
through the quality of resolution.
The directions were clear, the wind was free of dust,
a rain of flowers followed the sound of conch shells;
for all beings, moving and stationary,
that day of her birth brought happiness.
With that daughter, <s>Savitrī</s> (the mother)
shone even more, [the daughter] with a radiant halo;
like the earth far from [the foot of the mountain], at the sound of a fresh cloud,
with a newly sprouted streak of gems.
Day by day she grew,
like the crescent moon that has gained its rising,
nourishing special graces made of charm,
like the [moon nourishing] successive phases within its light.
Her relatives called her <s>Pārvatī</s>, a name befitting her lineage,
dear to her kinfolk.
When her mother forbade her from <s>tapas</s> (austerity) saying 'U mā!' (Oh, do not!),
the beautiful-faced one thereafter acquired the name <s>Umā</s>.
The gaze of the mountain lord, even though he had a son,
did not reach satisfaction upon that daughter;
indeed, on the mango tree of inexhaustible blossoms belonging to spring,
the garland of bees has a special attachment.
Like a lamp by the greatness of its radiance,
like the triple-pathed [Ganges] by [being] the path of heaven,
like a wise man by refined speech —

children.text: tayā sa pūtaś ca vibhūṣitaś ca
children.translated_text: by her, he was both purified and adorned.
On the sandy banks of the <s>Mandākinī</s>,
she played with balls and toy dolls,
positioned amidst her companions,
as if savoring the essence of play in childhood.
Like rows of geese [approaching] the <s>Gaṅgā</s> in autumn,
like the great herb [glowing] by its own light at night,
the sciences from previous births, when the time of instruction was firm,
came to her [of their own accord].
An ornament for the body's graceful form that needed no assembling,
a means of intoxication that had no need of wine,
a weapon of <s>Kāma</s> (Love) other than his flower[-arrows] —
she then attained the age beyond childhood.
Like a painting unveiled by the brush,
like a lotus opened by the sun's rays,
her form, shining with graceful symmetry,
became fully revealed by new youth.
Her two feet, by the luster of the raised toenails,
seeming to pour forth redness as they were set down,
brought to the earth
the transient beauty of a land-lotus.
She, with her gracefully bent limbs, by royal swans
whose steps were charmingly playful,
was followed — [swans] eager for instruction,
desirous of imitating the tinkling of her anklets.
Her two lovely calves, neither overly round
nor too long, having been fashioned [by the Creator],
it seemed as though the Creator's effort
in designing the remaining limbs was [especially directed] toward charm.
The trunks of the lord of elephants, due to roughness of skin;
the plantain stems, due to extreme coldness —
even having obtained a comparable form in the world,
became excluded from being similes for her thighs.
From this much alone the beauty of the blameless one
is to be inferred — the place of the girdle-string,
which was afterwards placed upon the lap of <s>Giriśa</s> (<s>Śiva</s>),
a lap not to be desired by any other woman.
Her slender new line of hair, entering the depression of her deep navel,
shone beautifully,
passing beyond the waist-cord, like a ray
from the central gem of that girdle, which was dark [in hue].
The young girl, slender-waisted with a waist like a sacrificial altar,
beautifully bore a triple fold [on her belly],
as if fashioned by new youth
as a stairway for <s>Kāma</s> (Love) to ascend.
The two breasts of that lotus-eyed one, pale [with fullness], had grown such
that they pressed against each other,
so that between the two, dark-tipped,
even the space of a lotus-fiber thread could not be found.
Her two arms, surpassing even the <s>śirīṣa</s> flower in delicacy —
this is my conjecture —
were fashioned by <s>Makaradhvaja</s> (the banner-bearing Love god), though himself defeated,
as nooses for the neck of <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>).
Between her neck, curved [gracefully toward] the breasts,
and the pearl necklace, lying flat [against it],
because each enhanced the beauty of the other,
the relationship of ornament and ornamented was mutual.
Having gone to the moon, [beauty] does not enjoy the qualities of the lotus;
and resting in the lotus, [it does not enjoy] the luster of the moon;
but having attained the face of <s>Umā</s>, the fickle
<s>Lakṣmī</s> (beauty) obtained the delight of a double abode.
If a flower were placed upon a coral sprout,
or a pearl were set upon bright coral,
then it might imitate that radiant smile of hers,
whose luster bordered on her copper-red lips.
When she spoke, her voice as if dripping with nectar,
she of noble speech —
even the <s>Cuckoo</s>, nourished by another, of discordant sound,
[felt] as if its strings were being struck for the listener.
The restless, sidelong glance of that long-eyed one,
indistinguishable from a blue lotus swaying in the breeze —
was it taken by her from the doe-eyed [deer],
or was it taken from her by the doe-eyed [deer]?
The beauty of her brows, with their curved lines,
as if drawn by a collyrium-stick —
seeing it, artful in its playfulness, <s>Anaṅga</s> (Love)
abandoned the pride in the beauty of his own bow.
If shame could exist in the minds of animals,
then surely, upon seeing the tresses of the daughter of the mountain-king,
the <s>Camarī</s> (yak-cows) would loosen
their fondness for their own tail-hair.
She was fashioned by the Creator with effort,
with the aggregate of all materials for comparison placed in their proper positions,
as if out of a desire
to see all beauty concentrated in one place.
<s>Nārada</s>, who roams freely, once upon a time,
having seen the girl in the presence of her father, it is said,
proclaimed that she would become the sole wife,
who would lovingly take half the body of <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>).
Her father, even though she had reached a bold age,
stood firm, with desire for any other suitor abandoned;
for fires other [than the sacrificial fire] do not deserve
the oblation that has been purified by <s>mantras</s>.
The mountain was not able to bestow his daughter
upon the god of gods who had not asked;
a virtuous person, out of fear of the rejection of a request,
maintains neutrality even regarding a desired object.
Ever since, in her previous birth, the beautiful-toothed one
had abandoned her body due to the anger of <s>Dakṣa</s>,
from that very time, the Lord of creatures (<s>Śiva</s>), free from attachment,
had become one without possessions.
He, clad in animal skin, self-controlled for <s>tapas</s> (austerity),
where the <s>devadāru</s> cedars were sprinkled by the current of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>,
on a plateau of the <s>Himālaya</s>, fragrant with musk,
with faintly singing <s>Kiṃnaras</s>, took up his abode.
His <s>gaṇas</s> (attendants), wearing the flowers born of <s>Meru</s> as ear-ornaments,
holding birch-bark sheets smooth to the touch,
speckled with <s>manaḥśilā</s> (realgar), seated themselves
upon rock-surfaces covered with tree-lichen.
A hump-backed bull, scraping with the tips of his hooves
the rocks compacted with snow, proud and spirited,
having been somehow spotted by startled <s>gavayas</s> (wild oxen),
bellowed, unable to endure the roar of a lion.
There, having kindled the sacrificial fire with kindling,
[<s>Śiva</s>], the eight-formed one, [feeding] his own other form,
himself the bestower of the fruits of <s>tapas</s>,
performed <s>tapas</s> driven by some desire.
The lord of the mountain, having honored with an <s>arghya</s> (offering) that priceless one
who is worshipped by the inhabitants of heaven,
for his [<s>Śiva</s>'s] service, dispatched his devoted daughter
together with her companions.
Though she was an obstacle to his meditation,
<s>Giriśa</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) accepted her, as she wished to serve him;
those whose minds are not disturbed even when a cause of disturbance is present —

children.text: yeṣāṃ na cetāṃsi ta eva dhīrāḥ
children.translated_text: they alone are truly steadfast.
Having gathered flowers for the offering, skilled in sweeping the sacrificial ground,
and bringing water for the observance-rites and the <s>kuśa</s> grass,
that beautiful-haired one served <s>Giriśa</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) every day,
her fatigue restrained by the [cooling] moonbeams from his crest.
At that time, oppressed
by <s>Tāraka</s> [the demon], the gods
placing <s>Bṛhaspati</s> (<s>Turāsāha</s>) at their head,
went to the abode of the Self-born (<s>Brahmā</s>).
<s>Brahmā</s> appeared before them,
whose facial luster had faded —
like the sun [appearing] in the morning before ponds
whose lotuses are closed in sleep.
Then they all [approached] the Ordainer of all,
the all-faced one,
the Lord of speech, with meaningful words,
having bowed down, they stood [before him].
Obeisance to you of triple form,
who before creation were pure spirit alone,
who, for the division into the three <s>guṇas</s> (qualities),
afterwards attained differentiation.
That which was the infallible seed sown by you,
O Unborn One, within the waters —
from that [arose] this entire universe, moving and unmoving;
you are celebrated as its origin.
You, through three states,
proclaiming your greatness,
have become the single cause
of dissolution, preservation, and creation.
Woman and man are portions of yourself,
your form divided with the desire to create;
those two, the shares of procreation,
are remembered as the parents of creation.
By the measure of your own time,
you whose night and day are distributed —
your sleep and waking
are the dissolution and arising of beings.
You are the womb of the world, yet yourself without a womb;
the end of the world, yet yourself without end;
the beginning of the world, yet yourself without beginning;
the lord of the world, yet yourself without a lord.
You know yourself by yourself;
you create yourself by yourself.
By your own accomplished self
you dissolve into yourself alone.
Fluid, hardened by aggregation,
gross, subtle, light, heavy,
manifest, and more than manifest — you are [all these];
you have mastery over your divine powers.
The <s>Praṇava</s> (the syllable Oṃ) is their opening,
their utterance is through the three proper methods,
their action is sacrifice (<s>yajña</s>), their fruit is heaven —
of those sacred utterances, you are the source.
They call you <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature),
the impeller toward the goals of a person;
they know you as the witness thereof, the detached
<s>Puruṣa</s> (supreme person) — you yourself.
You are the father even of the ancestors,
the deity even of the gods,
you are the beyond even of the beyond,
the creator even of the creators.
You yourself are the oblation and the offerer,
the food and the eater, eternally,
you are what is to be known and the knower,
the meditator and that supreme object of meditation.
Having heard from them these praises,
truthful and touching the heart,
the Creator, inclined toward grace,
replied to the celestials.
Of that ancient poet [<s>Brahmā</s>],
uttered from the four mouths,
there issued forth the fourfold flow of words
that fulfilled its purpose.
Welcome to you who have arrived,
relying on your respective powers and
jurisdictions, simultaneously, from the arms of the ages —
you of mighty valor.
Why is it that your faces
do not bear their own radiance as before,
like luminaries whose light
has been dimmed by frost?
Because of the subsidence of its flames, this
thunderbolt that has not discharged the weapon of the gods —
the thunderbolt of <s>Vṛtra</s>'s slayer —
appears as if its splendor has been blunted.
And why has this noose of <s>Pracetas</s> [<s>Varuṇa</s>],
irresistible to foes, [now] in his hand
assumed the pitiable state of a serpent
whose power has been destroyed by a mantra?
The arm of <s>Kubera</s>, with its mace cast aside,
seems to declare the humiliation
that is a thorn in his heart,
like a tree with a broken branch.
<s>Yama</s> too, scratching the earth
with his staff whose splendor has set,
treats this [staff], though infallible,
with the lightness of an extinguished torch.
And how have these <s>Āditya</s>s (sun-gods),
cooled by the diminishing of their radiance,
come to be gazed at freely
as if painted in a picture?
From the agitation of the <s>Marut</s>s (wind-gods),
the breaking of their speed is inferred,
as if from the damming of waters
by their flowing upstream.
With topknots of matted hair bent down
and the tips of their crescent moons hanging low,
even the heads of the <s>Rudra</s>s
betray their wounded pride.
You who first gained your positions —
how have you been displaced by those more powerful,
like general rules set aside
by exceptions?
Then tell me, children, what you seek
having come hither assembled together,
for in me lies the creation of the worlds,
and in you their protection is established.
Then, with his thousand eyes
adorned like lotus-pools stirred by gentle breezes,
<s>Vāsava</s> [<s>Indra</s>] urged
the preceptor [to speak].
He, two-eyed, yet surpassing the thousand eyes
of <s>Hari</s>'s [<s>Indra</s>'s] sight,
<s>Vācaspati</s> [<s>Bṛhaspati</s>], with palms joined,
spoke thus to the lotus-seated one [<s>Brahmā</s>]:
Even as you say, O blessed one,
our position has been trampled by our foes —
you who attend to each [god] individually,
how will you not know this, O lord?
Emboldened by a boon obtained from you,
the great demon named <s>Tāraka</s>
has risen for the destruction of the worlds
like a comet.
In his city, the sun extends only so much
heat as is sufficient
for the opening of the lotuses
in the garden-pools.
The moon attends upon him at all times
with all his digits,
except for the single crescent
that has been made a crest-jewel by <s>Hara</s> [<s>Śiva</s>].
Avoiding his path in the garden,
for fear of being accused of stealing flowers,
the wind does not blow near him
more than a palm-leaf fan.
Abandoning their service by turns,
intent upon gathering flowers,
the seasons attend upon him
like ordinary garden-keepers.
The lord of rivers [the ocean] keeps
gems fit to be his offerings
under the waters with great difficulty,
waiting until their full formation.
And serpents led by <s>Vāsuki</s>,
with blazing gem-crests, at night
attend upon him
having become steady lamps.
Even <s>Indra</s>, seeking favors granted by him,
repeatedly propitates him
with ornaments from the wish-fulfilling trees
brought by messengers.
Though thus worshipped,
he torments the three worlds;
a wicked person is pacified by retaliation,
not by kindness.
By him, the trees of <s>Nandana</s> [garden],
whose shoots had been tenderly plucked by the hands of celestial women,
are made to know
the blows of the axe.
For when he sleeps, he is fanned
by <s>cāmara</s> (fly-whisks) wielded by captive celestial women,
whose breezes mingle with their sighs
and shower droplets of tears.
Having uprooted the peaks of <s>Meru</s>,
trodden by the hooves of the horses of the sun,
he has fashioned them into pleasure-mountains
in his own mansions.
The water remaining in the <s>Mandākinī</s>,
muddied by the ichor of the elephants of the quarters —
that is now the state of its pools
with their golden lotuses.
The joy of beholding the [three] worlds
is not experienced by the celestials,
since the path of their aerial chariots has become impassable
through fear of his attack.
The oblations gathered by sacrificers
in extended sacrifices —
that deceiver snatches them from us
right from the mouths of the sacred fire.
By him, <s>Uccaiḥśravas</s>, the jewel among horses,
was carried away on high,
like the glory long acquired by <s>Indra</s>
that was bound to his body.
Against that cruel one, all our stratagems
have had their efficacy thwarted,
like potent medicines
in a disease of combined humors.
And where our hope of victory lay —
the discus of <s>Hari</s> [<s>Viṣṇu</s>], blazing with flames from the impact —
he has worn it on his neck
like an ornamental disc.
His elephants, having defeated <s>Airāvata</s>,
now practice [their skill of] striking riverbanks
on the <s>Puṣkarāvartaka</s> and other
rain-clouds.
Therefore, O lord, we desire a commander-in-chief created [by you]
for his destruction,
as those desirous of liberation [desire] <s>dharma</s>
that severs the bondage of <s>karma</s> — from <s>Bhava</s> [<s>Śiva</s>] himself.
A protector of the armies of the gods —
placing whom at the fore, the mountain-splitter [<s>Indra</s>]
will bring back from the enemies
the goddess of victory, like a captive.
When that speech had ended,
the Self-born [<s>Brahmā</s>] uttered a voice
that surpassed in felicity
rain [falling] after thunder.
This desire of yours shall be fulfilled;
let some time be awaited.
But for its accomplishment, I shall not personally
undertake the labor of creation.
On the other hand, this demon who has attained glory
deserves to meet his end only [in the proper way];
even a poison-tree, having nurtured [it],
it is improper to cut down oneself.
This very [boon] was chosen by him,
and was promised by me to him —
his austerity, pacified by the boon,
was sufficient to burn the worlds.
In battle, who could withstand that one
risen in martial fury,
except a portion born from the seed
of the blue-throated one [<s>Śiva</s>]?
For that god is the supreme light
established beyond darkness,
whose power cannot be fully measured
either by me or by <s>Viṣṇu</s>.
With the form of <s>Umā</s>, you should strive
to draw out the mind of <s>Śambhu</s> [<s>Śiva</s>],
stilled by self-restraint,
as a loadstone [draws] iron.
Both are capable of bearing
the power deposited by them both —
she, or that watery form
of <s>Śambhu</s>'s that is mine.
His own [son], attaining the generalship
of the blue-throated one [<s>Śiva</s>], for you,
will release the braids of the captive celestial women
by the splendors of his valor.
Having spoken thus to the gods,
the source of the universe [<s>Brahmā</s>] vanished;
and they too, with their duties fixed in mind,
returned to heaven.
There, having decided upon <s>Kandarpa</s> [the god of love],
<s>Pākaśāsana</s> [<s>Indra</s>] went [to him],
with a mind whose speed was doubled
by the urgency of accomplishing the task.
Then he, with his bow — charming, curved like the graceful eyebrow-creeper of a beautiful woman,
bearing the mark of <s>Rati</s>'s bracelet — hung upon his neck,
his arrows being mango-sprouts placed in the hand of his companion <s>Madhu</s> [Spring],
the flower-bowed one [<s>Kāma</s>], stood before the thousand-eyed [<s>Indra</s>] with palms joined.
When <s>Maghona</s> [<s>Indra</s>] looked at him, leaving aside the other gods,
his thousand eyes fell upon [him] all at once —
for the respect of the mighty toward their dependents
generally wavers according to the need [they serve].
He [<s>Kāma</s>], granted a seat near the throne by <s>Vāsava</s> [<s>Indra</s>]
with the words 'sit here,'
acknowledging the master's grace with a bow of his head,
began to speak to him privately thus:
Command, O you who know the distinctions among men,
what task of yours there is in the worlds;
I desire the favor, prompted by your remembrance [of me],
to be enhanced by your command.
Who is that envious rival coveting your position
who has been produced by prolonged and extreme austerities,
who would remain obedient
to this bow of mine with arrow fitted?
Who, disapproved [by you], has taken to the path of liberation
out of fear of the afflictions of rebirth?
Let him remain long bound
by the sidelong glances of beautiful women, clever with arched eyebrows.
Of your enemy who was taught statecraft
even by <s>Uśanas</s> [<s>Śukra</s>] — tell me, whose
wealth and virtue shall I assail,
like a swollen flood [assails] the banks of a river?
Which woman, devoted to the vow of faithfulness to one husband,
into whose [heart] the fickle mind has entered through her beauty —
do you wish [me to make her] a woman of full hips, shameless,
with her arms clasped around a neck in self-chosen embrace?
By which lover have you been spurned,
when you bowed at her feet, shaken off by the angry one —
in whose [body] I shall cause deep remorse,
a body seeking refuge on a bed of coral [sprouts]?
Be pleased! Let the thunderbolt rest, O hero!
Which enemy of the gods, struck by my arrows,
shall not tremble, his arm-strength rendered vain,
even before women with anger-quivering lips?
By your grace, even I, the flower-weaponed one,
having obtained <s>Madhu</s> [Spring] alone as ally,
could shatter the composure even of <s>Hara</s> [<s>Śiva</s>], the wielder of <s>Pināka</s> —
who are the other bowmen compared to me?
Then, lowering his foot from his thigh
onto a footstool honored by that contact,
<s>Ākhaṇḍala</s> [<s>Indra</s>] spoke thus to <s>Kāma</s>,
revealing his own power regarding the intended purpose:
All this befits you, friend;
both are my weapons — the thunderbolt and you;
the thunderbolt is blunted against those great in the power of austerity,
but you are all-pervading and effective.

children.text: avaimi te sāram ataḥ khalu tvāṃ
children.translated_text: I know your essence; therefore indeed
I shall employ you, my equal, in a weighty task;
<s>Śeṣa</s> is appointed to bear the earth,
considering [his capacity for] supporting it, by <s>Kṛṣṇa</s> [<s>Viṣṇu</s>].
Aiming the flight of your arrows at the bull-bannered one [<s>Śiva</s>],
you must do our work — [which is] as good as accomplished [by you];
know now the desire of those who share
the portions of sacrifice — this very thing against the lofty foes.
For these gods desire a general for victory
born from the power of <s>Bhava</s> [<s>Śiva</s>];
and that [birth] is to be accomplished by a single arrow-strike of yours —
[a son] born from <s>Brahmā</s>'s own limb, his mind united with <s>Brahman</s>.
Strive to make the devoted daughter of the <s>Himālaya</s>
pleasing to that self-controlled one;
she alone is the worthy ground for the deposition of his seed
among women — thus has the Self-born [<s>Brahmā</s>] instructed.
And by her father's command, the daughter of the mountain-king
has been attending upon <s>Sthāṇu</s> [<s>Śiva</s>] as he practices austerity on the plateau —
so I have heard from the mouths of the <s>Apsaras</s>es;
that group [of Apsarases] is my intelligence-network.
Then go for success; accomplish the work of the gods;
this purpose requires yet another purpose [to be fulfilled first];
it awaits you as the supreme catalyst,
as a seed-sprout [awaits] water before germination.
In that stratagem for the victory of the gods,
you alone are expert, for the flight of the arrow is your name;
for the glory of men lies indeed
in a deed shared by no other.
The gods are the supplicants here;
the task concerns all three worlds;
and the work of your bow is not excessively violent —
ah, your prowess is truly enviable!
<s>Madhu</s> [Spring], O <s>Manmatha</s>, is your companion
by natural alliance, even without being told;
who commands the wind
to be the inciter of fire?
Accepting his master's command with 'so be it,'
as if it were the remaining [easy] part, <s>Madana</s> [<s>Kāma</s>] set forth;
with a hand roughened by the striking of <s>Airāvata</s>,
<s>Indra</s> touched his body [in farewell].
He, accompanied by his beloved companion
<s>Mādhava</s> [Spring] and by <s>Rati</s> who followed apprehensively,
seeking the accomplishment of a task at the cost of his own body,
went to the hermitage of <s>Sthāṇu</s> [<s>Śiva</s>] in the <s>Himālaya</s>.
In that forest, working against
the concentration of austerity of the self-restrained sages,
Spring blossomed forth, assuming himself to be
the embodied pride of the desire-born [<s>Kāma</s>].
When the sun, transgressing the [proper] season,
began to move toward the direction guarded by <s>Kubera</s> [the north],
the southern direction released from its mouth a fragrant breeze
like a feigned sigh.
The <s>Aśoka</s> tree suddenly brought forth flowers
with sprouts right from the trunk itself,
and did not wait for the contact
of the tinkling-anklet-adorned foot of beautiful women.
On the newly-sprouted mango arrow, beautiful with leaves like fresh coral shoots,
brought to completion,
[Spring] settled the sweet bees
as if inscribing the letters of the name of <s>Manobhava</s> (the god of love).
The <s>karṇikāra</s> (Pterospermum) tree, though excelling in color,
pained the heart by its lack of fragrance;
for generally, in the arrangement of a full complement of qualities,
the disposition of the Creator turns away.
The <s>palāśa</s> (Butea) blossoms, deep red,
remained curved like the crescent moon because of their unopened state,
like the nail-marks of the forest-lands
freshly united with Spring.
The beauty of Spring, variegated by the lines of clinging black bees as collyrium-marks,
displaying a <s>tilaka</s> (ornamental mark) on [Spring's] face,
adorned the lips with the mango-sprouts,
delicate as the early dawn's reddish hue.
The deer, their gaze obstructed
by pollen-grains from the flower-clusters of the <s>priyāla</s> (Buchanania) tree,
intoxicated, roamed against the breeze
through the forest-lands, releasing rustling leaves.
The male cuckoo, his throat astringent from tasting mango sprouts,
sang sweetly —
that very [song] became the speech of <s>Smara</s> (Love),
skilled in destroying the composure of steadfast women.
With the departure of winter, the perspiration
of the <s>Kiṃpuruṣa</s> women, whose lips were clear
and whose facial complexions had become slightly pale,
left its mark on the ornamental leaf-designs [painted on their cheeks].
The ascetics dwelling in the grove of <s>Sthāṇu</s> (Śiva),
beholding that untimely onset of Spring,
with their transformations restrained by effort,
somehow remained masters of their minds.
When <s>Madana</s> (Love), with his flower-bow strung,
accompanied by <s>Rati</s> as his second, had entered that region,
the couples revealed their passion through their actions,
pervaded by the resinous sap that had risen in the wood.
The bee drank honey from a single flower-cup,
followed by his beloved;
and the black antelope scratched with his horn
the doe whose eyes closed at his touch.
The she-elephant gave the bull-elephant
a mouthful of water fragrant with lotus pollen, out of affection;
and the bird named <s>Rathāṅga</s> (the cakravāka) honored his mate
with a half-eaten lotus stalk.
In the intervals between songs, with drops of sweat of exertion
slightly smudging the painted leaf-design [on her cheek],
the <s>Kiṃpuruṣa</s> kissed the face of his beloved,
beautiful with eyes rolling from the intoxication of flower-wine.
Even the trees received from the creeper-brides,
whose flower-clusters formed their breasts and whose quivering sprouts were charming lips,
embraces of their bowing
branch-arms.
Even having heard the song of the <s>Apsaras</s> at this moment,
<s>Hara</s> (Śiva) remained absorbed in meditation;
for obstacles born of the disruption of <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption)
never arise for those who are masters of themselves.
Then <s>Nandī</s>, standing at the door of the bower,
with a golden staff resting on his left forearm,
restrained the <s>gaṇas</s> (attendants) with merely the gesture
of a single finger placed on his lips — 'Do not be restless!'
Motionless the trees, hushed the bees,
silent the birds, still the movement of animals —
by his command, the entire forest
stood as if it were a scene begun on a canvas.
Avoiding the line of his sight, <s>Kāma</s> (Love),
like the planet <s>Śukra</s> (Venus) going ahead on a march,
entered the seat of meditation of the Lord of Beings,
where the branches of the bending <s>Nameru</s> tree interlocked at the edges.
On a platform of <s>devadāru</s> (deodar) trees,
covered with a tiger skin,
he beheld <s>Tryambaka</s> (the three-eyed Śiva), the self-controlled one,
seated, with his body nearly touching the ground.
His upper body steady in the lotus-posture,
erect and extended, with both shoulders drawn in,
because of the placement of his two palms facing upward,
his lap was like a full-blown lotus.
His mass of matted hair raised by a serpent,
a doubled rosary of <s>akṣa</s> (Elaeocarpus) beads hung from his ear,
wearing a knotted black antelope skin
that was specially dark from contact with the luster of his throat.
With his fierce pupils slightly luminous yet motionless,
disengaged from any movement of the brows,
his eyes with unblinking rows of lashes,
with downward rays focused on the tip of his nose.
Like a rain-cloud withholding the onset of rain,
like a reservoir of water without a ripple,
because of the restraint of the inner breaths,
like a lamp undisturbed in a windless place.
With shoots of light that found their path through the space
between the skull-bowl and the eyes, rising from his head,
he was dimming the beauty of the crescent moon,
more delicate than a lotus-fiber thread.
His mind, its activity barred from the nine doors [of the body],
established in the heart and subject to <s>samādhi</s>,
he was contemplating within himself that <s>ātman</s>
which the knowers of the field know as the imperishable.
<s>Smara</s> (Love), seeing the odd-eyed one in such a state,
unapproachable even by the mind from nearby,
did not notice, his hand faltering with apprehension,
the arrow and bow slipping from his own hand.
Then, as if rekindling his power
which was mostly extinguished, by her bodily charm,
the daughter of the Mountain King appeared,
accompanied by the two forest-deities.
Wearing the spring-flower ornaments —
<s>aśoka</s> blossoms that put rubies to shame,
<s>karṇikāra</s> flowers that rivaled the luster of gold,
<s>sinduvāra</s> flowers fashioned into a pearl necklace.
Slightly bent forward by her breasts,
wearing a garment the color of the young sun,
bowed down with abundant clusters of flowers,
she moved like a blossoming creeper.
Repeatedly adjusting the girdle of stamen-garlands
that had slipped from her hips,
placed there by <s>Smara</s> (Love) who knew the right spot —
as if it were a second bowstring for his bow.
A bee, drawn close to her <s>bimba</s>-fruit lips,
its desire increased by the fragrance of her breath,
she warded off with a play-lotus,
her gaze darting with agitation at every moment.
Seeing her, faultless in every limb,
inspiring bashfulness even in <s>Rati</s> (the goddess of love),
the flower-bowed one once again
hoped for the success of his mission against the conqueror of the senses, the trident-bearer.
<s>Umā</s>, [destined to be] the future wife of <s>Śambhu</s>,
reached the threshold of attendance upon the ascetic;
and he, through <s>yoga</s>, having seen within the supreme light
known as the Supreme Self, ceased [his meditation].
Then, the ground somehow supported by the tips
of the hoods of the lord of serpents below,
the Lord slowly released his breath
and broke the firm lotus-posture.
<s>Nandī</s>, bowing, announced to him
the arrival of the mountain's daughter for service;
and he ushered her in to his master,
whose permission to enter was granted by a mere raising of the brow.
At her feet, preceded by prostration,
by her two companions, flowers of the late winter
plucked by their own hands
were scattered — an offering of blossoms mixed with broken sprigs — at the base of <s>Tryambaka</s>'s (Śiva's) feet.
<s>Umā</s> too, letting fall a fresh <s>karṇikāra</s> flower
that graced the middle of her dark tresses,
made obeisance with her head to the one whose banner bears the bull,
using the shoot that had fallen from her ear.
'May you obtain a husband devoted to none other' —
she was thus truly blessed by <s>Bhava</s> (Śiva);
for never do the utterances of the Lord
bear a contrary meaning in the world.
<s>Kāma</s>, meanwhile, awaiting the opportunity for his arrow,
like a moth wishing to enter the mouth of fire,
with his aim fixed on <s>Hara</s> in <s>Umā</s>'s presence,
repeatedly fingered the string of his bow.
Then <s>Gaurī</s> (Pārvatī) presented to <s>Giriśa</s> (Śiva),
the ascetic, with her coppery-hued hand,
a rosary of lotus seeds from the <s>Mandākinī</s>,
dried by the rays of the sun.
The three-eyed one began to receive it,
out of fondness for his affectionate devotee;
and the flower-weaponed one (<s>Kāma</s>) fitted to his bow
the infallible arrow called <s>Saṃmohana</s> (Bewilderment).
<s>Hara</s>, his composure slightly disturbed,
like the ocean at the onset of moonrise,
turned his eyes upon <s>Umā</s>'s face
with its <s>bimba</s>-fruit lower lip.
The mountain's daughter too, revealing her feelings
through her limbs like quivering young <s>kadamba</s> flowers,
stood turned sideways, with her face
even more lovely, her eyes averted.
Then the odd-eyed one, by force of self-mastery,
powerfully restraining the agitation of his senses once more,
wishing to see the cause of the disturbance of his mind,
cast his gaze to the edges of the quarters.
He saw, with fist planted at the corner of his right eye,
shoulder bent, left foot drawn up,
his beautiful bow drawn in a circle,
his own origin (<s>Kāma</s>) poised to strike.
Of him whose anger swelled at the affront to his <s>tapas</s> (asceticism),
whose face was terrible to behold because of the frown of his brows,
from his third eye, a flickering flame
of fire, they say, suddenly fell forth.
'Lord, withdraw your anger, withdraw!' —
while these words of the wind-gods were still traveling through the sky,
that fire born from the eye of <s>Bhava</s> (Śiva)
reduced <s>Madana</s> (Love) to mere ashes.
By the delusion born from intense attachment,
which paralyzes the activity of the senses,
<s>Rati</s>, unaware of her husband's calamity, for a moment
seemed as though she had rendered a service [to him].
The ascetic, having swiftly struck down that obstacle to his <s>tapas</s>
as a thunderbolt [strikes] a tree,
wishing to avoid the proximity of a woman,
the Lord of Beings vanished together with his attendants.
The mountain's daughter too, deeming her father's lofty aspiration

children.text: vyarthaṃ samarthya lalitaṃ vapur ātmanaś ca
children.translated_text: to be in vain, and her own lovely form [likewise futile],
and all the more ashamed because it was before her two friends,
departed, empty, heading homeward, somehow.
At once, the mountain, taking in his arms
his pitiable daughter whose eyes were shut in terror of <s>Rudra</s>'s wrath,
like the divine elephant holding a lotus caught on its tusk,
retraced his path, his body elongated by his speed.
Then <s>Rati</s>, the wife of <s>Kāma</s>, who had been overcome by delusion
and rendered helpless, was awakened
by Fate, which was about to inflict upon her
the unbearable suffering of fresh widowhood.
She opened her eyes, like [eyes] unclosing
at the end of dissolution,
and those unsatisfied [eyes] did not find
her beloved, whose sight was utterly lost.
'O lord of my life, are you alive?' — exclaiming thus,
having risen, she saw before her
on the ground, in the shape of a man,
nothing but ashes from the fire of <s>Hara</s>'s anger.
Then she, once again overwhelmed,
her breasts dusty from embracing the ground,
lamented with her hair disheveled,
as if making the earth share her sorrow.
'That body of yours which, by its beauty,
had been the standard of comparison for graceful women,
has come to this condition —
am I not torn apart? Truly, women are hard-hearted!'
'Where, having abandoned me whose life depends on you,
with your friendship broken in an instant,
have you fled — like a mass of water
when the embankment of a lotus pond is breached?'
'You did nothing disagreeable to me,

children.text: pratikūlaṃ na ca te mayā kṛtam
children.translated_text: nor did I do anything contrary to you;
why, then, without cause, is a sight of you
not granted to me as I lament?'
'Do you remember, O Love, the bindings with girdle-strings
when my name slipped from your lips?
Or the blows of the ear-lotus
that stained the eyes with fallen pollen?'
'That you said — "You dwell in my heart" — that, my beloved,
I now know to be deceit;
if this were not a mere figure of speech,
how are you bodiless while <s>Rati</s> is unharmed?'
'I shall follow the path of you,
a new traveler to the other world;
by Fate is this world deceived —
for the happiness of embodied beings depends on you.'
'On the city streets, veiled by the darkness of night,
agitated by the rumbling of clouds,
who but you, O beloved, has the power
to guide lovers' beloveds to their dwelling?'
'Rolling the reddened eyes,
stammering words at every step —
without you, the intoxication of wine
is now but a mockery for lovely women.'
'Having understood that the body of your dear friend [the moon]
has been rendered to mere story,
even after the passing of the full moon,
the moonbeam, O Bodiless One, will shed its grief [by waning] into thinness.'
'The new mango blossom — beautifully bound with fresh green and red,
heralded by the sweet sounds of cuckoos —
tell me, whose arrow
will it now become?'
'The rows of bees that you employed
again and again as strings for your bow —
with their plaintive, piteous humming,
they seem to weep in sympathy with my great sorrow.'
'Having regained your beautiful body,
arise once more and assign
the cuckoo, naturally skilled in sweet speech,
to be <s>Rati</s>'s messenger!'
'The lovemaking in secret — sought with bowed head,
the embraces with trembling —
remember, remembering those, O Love,

children.text: smara saṃsmṛtya na śāntir asti me
children.translated_text: there is no peace for me!'
'This vernal [makeup], fashioned on my limbs
by you, expert in love,
the flower-ornament still remains,

children.text: tava tac cāru vapur na dṛśyate
children.translated_text: but your beautiful body is not to be seen.'
You who were invoked by the cruel gods
while the adornment was still incomplete —
Make this, the left
foot, reddened with lac-dye, and come to me.
Having returned by the path of the sun,
I shall again rest in your lap,
before you are seduced by the skillful
celestial women in heaven, O beloved.
<s>Rati</s>, deprived of <s>Madana</s> (the god of love),
will live only for a moment — this is
my firm resolve to be declared,
O beloved, even though I follow you [in death].
How shall I perform the final adornment
for you who are separated from me by the other world?
You have gone to an unforeseen
destination, at once in body and in life.
I remember you straightening
the arrow, with the bow resting on your lap,
the conversation with <s>Madhu</s> (Spring) accompanied by smiles,
and the sidelong glances from the corners of your eyes.
Where now is your heart-winning friend
<s>Madhu</s> (Spring), whose bow was strung with flowers?
Surely he has not been sent
by the fiercely wrathful <s>Pinākin</s> (Śiva) to the fate of a departed friend?
Then, pierced by those syllables of lamentation
like arrows smeared [with poison] on the heart,
<s>Madhu</s> (Spring) revealed himself before
the anguished <s>Rati</s>, [coming] to console her.
Seeing him, she wept profusely
and struck her breast-pressed chest,
for the grief of one's own people, when present before one,
arises as if through an open door.
And thus, distressed, she spoke to him:
'O friend, <s>Vasanta</s> (Spring), see what remains —
these ashes, mottled grey like a dove,
scattered particle by particle by the winds.'
'O, now grant a vision of yourself,
O <s>Smara</s> (Love), this <s>Mādhava</s> (Spring) is anxious for you.',
The love of men toward their beloved is inconstant,
but not so toward a dear friend.
With this [friend] standing at your side,
you made the world, with its gods and demons, obey your command —
through your bow whose string was a lotus fiber,
armed with arrows of delicate flowers.
That friend of yours, gone, does not return,
like a lamp struck by the wind.
I am his condition — look at me,
ruined by unbearable calamity.
Fate has wrought a half-slaughter,
by releasing me from death along with <s>Kāma</s> (Love),
for even a blameless creeper
is destined to fall when the tree it clings to is broken by an elephant.
Therefore, let this be done next —
this duty to a kinswoman, by you:
by releasing me to the fire,
deliver me, desolate, to the presence of my husband.
Moonlight departs with the moon,
lightning dissolves with the cloud;
that women follow the path of their husbands
is acknowledged even by the unconscious [elements].
With my breasts anointed with this
auspicious ash from the body of my beloved,
I shall lay my body in the fire
as if on a bed of fresh shoots.
O gentle one, you have many times assisted us both
in strewing flowers;
now quickly prepare for me
a funeral pyre — I beseech you with folded hands.
Then hasten the fire I have offered
by fanning it with the southern breeze,
for you well know that <s>Smara</s> (Love)

children.text: kṣaṇam apy utsahate na māṃ vinā
children.translated_text: cannot bear even a moment without me.
And having done this, let a single
offering of water be given for us both,
for without dividing [the offering] from me,
that kinsman of yours in the other world will drink it together with me.
And for the rites of the other world, O <s>Mādhava</s> (Spring),
addressing <s>Smara</s> (Love), [you should] offer
mango blossoms with trembling sprouts,
for your friend was born from the dear mango tree.
Then, to <s>Rati</s>, who was resolved to abandon her life,
a voice (<s>Sarasvatī</s>) from the sky
showed compassion, as the first rain
to a fish distressed by the drying of the lake.
'O wife of the flower-weaponed one, your husband
will not long be unattainable.',
'Hear by what deed he went
to the state of a moth in the flame of <s>Hara</s>'s (Śiva's) eye.'
<s>Prajāpati</s> (the Creator), with his senses aroused,
conceived desire for his own daughter.
Then, by that one (Śiva) who restrained [Prajāpati's] transgression,
[Kāma] was cursed — and he experienced this fruit [of that curse].
'When <s>Hara</s> (Śiva), inclined toward her through her austerities,
will marry <s>Pārvatī</s>,
then, having obtained happiness, he will
restore <s>Smara</s> (Love) to his own bodily form.'
And thus spoke the voice — entreated by <s>Dharma</s> —
granting the limit of <s>Smara</s>'s (Love's) curse,
for both the thunderbolt and nectar,
and [both] the self-controlled ones and the clouds have a single source.
'Therefore, O beautiful one, preserve this body
destined for a joyful reunion with your beloved,
for a river, its water drunk by the sun in summer,
is again joined with a flood [at the end of the dry season].'

children.text: itthaṃ rateḥ kim api bhūtam adṛśyarūpaṃ
children.translated_text: Thus, some invisible being
weakened <s>Rati</s>'s resolve to die,
and because of that assurance, the friend of the flower-weaponed one (<s>Vasanta</s>)
consoled her with words whose syllables conveyed virtuous meaning.
Then the wife of <s>Madana</s> (Love), emaciated by grief,
waited for the end of her calamity,
like the crescent of the daytime moon,
dimmed by the diminishing of its rays, [waiting for] the evening.
Thus, when the destroyer of <s>Manobhava</s> (Love), <s>Pinākin</s> (Śiva),
burned <s>Kāma</s> before her eyes, <s>Satī</s> (Pārvatī), her hopes shattered,
reproached her own beauty in her heart,
for charm bears fruit only when it pleases the beloved.
She desired to make her beauty not fruitless
by undertaking austerities, having resolved upon concentration;
for how else can one attain both —
such a love and such a husband?
And hearing that she, her mind attached to <s>Girīśa</s> (Śiva),
was resolved upon austerities,
<s>Menā</s> (her mother) embraced her to her bosom and spoke,
trying to dissuade her daughter from the great ascetic vow:
'The desired deities can be [worshipped] at home too, O child;

children.text: tapaḥ kva vatse kva ca tāvakaṃ vapuḥ
children.translated_text: what [need for] austerities, and what [comparison with] your body?
A <s>śirīṣa</s> blossom might bear the tread of a bee,
but not that of a bird.'
Thus instructing her daughter whose wish was fixed,
<s>Menā</s> was unable to restrain her from the endeavor;
who can turn back a mind firmly resolved upon its desired goal,
or water flowing downward?
Once, the wise [<s>Pārvatī</s>], through a friend who was near,
asked her father, who knew her heart's desire,
for permission to dwell in the forest,
for the purpose of austerities until the fruition of their result.
Then, having received permission from her exalted father,
who was pleased by her befitting resolve,
<s>Gaurī</s> went to a peak adorned with peacocks,
later renowned among people by her name.
Removing her necklace, she of unshakable resolve,
with her sandal paste wiped away by the supple stalk [of a brush],
bound on a bark garment, reddish-brown like the young dawn,
its fastenings loosened by the swell of her breasts.
Just as her face was beautiful with her well-known sweet tresses,
so too was it with matted locks;
a lotus shines not only with rows of bees,
but also when entwined with moss.
For the vow, she wore a triple girdle of <s>muñja</s> grass
which made her body shiver at every moment;
that [girdle], tied where the previous one had been bound,
made the place where her jeweled girdle-string had been seem [adorned] with passion.
Her hand, [once] turned away from the lip that had released its coloring
and from the ball reddened with the pigment from her breasts,
its fingers scratched from picking up <s>kuśa</s> grass shoots,
was made intimate with a rosary by her.
She who used to be distressed even by the flowers
from her own hair falling on a luxurious bed as she turned,
now slept using only her arm as a pillow,
seated on nothing but bare ground.
By her, steadfast in her vow, both [her charms] were deposited
as if entrusted to two [keepers] — to be taken back again:
her graceful movements to the slender creepers,
and her tremulous glances to the doe-eyed deer.
She herself, untiring, nurtured the young trees
with the streams flowing from her water-pot's breast,
for even <s>Guha</s> (<s>Kārttikeya</s>), for whom these were the first-born [children],
would not set aside his maternal affection [for them].
And the deer grew so trusting of her,
cherished by her offerings of handfuls of forest seeds,
that with their restless eyes, out of curiosity,
they measured their own eyes against hers in the presence of her companions.
Having performed her ablutions, having offered oblations to the fire,
clad in a bark upper-garment, engaged in study —
sages came wishing to see her;
for in those advanced in <s>dharma</s> (virtue), age is not considered.
That grove of austerities became purifying:
with trees that had shed their former jealousy toward rival beings and honored guests with desired fruits,
with fire maintained within new hermitage huts.
When she judged that the desired fruit
was not attainable by her previous level of austerity,
then, disregarding the tenderness of her own body,
she commenced to practice great austerities.
She who used to become exhausted even from playing with a ball —
by her, the practices of the sages were entered into.
Surely her body, fashioned of golden lotuses,
was soft by nature yet firm in essence.

children.text: mṛdu prakṛtyā ca sasāram eva ca

children.translated_text: In the pure [season], amidst four blazing sacred fires,
she of the pure smile and slender waist, standing in the center,
having conquered the radiance that repels the eye,
gazed at the sun with unwavering sight.
Her face, thus heated by the rays of the sun,
maintained the beauty of a lotus;
only at the outer corners of her long eyes
was a trace of darkening slowly produced.
Only water that came unsolicited,
and the rays of the moon, lord of plants, full of nectar —
these constituted her manner of breaking the fast,
with no means beyond subsisting like a tree.
Thoroughly heated by manifold fires —
the celestial [sun] and those fed with fuel —
and sprinkled at the end of summer with fresh rain,
she released upward-rising steam together with the earth.
The first raindrops, resting a moment on her eyelashes,
striking her lower lip, shattered on the slope of her breasts,
stumbling in her [belly's] folds,
reached her navel only after a long time.
The nights, with unceasing lightning flashes,
amid continuous rains and winds between them,
observed her — dwelling on a rock slab, shelterless —
as if standing witness to her great austerity.
She passed the nights of the cold month <s>Sahya</s>,
with winds scattering extreme snow, devoted to night-vigils,
compassionate, before a pair of <s>cakravāka</s> birds
separated and crying out to each other.
With her face — fragrant as a lotus, at night,
beautiful with her trembling lower lip like a petal —
she seemed to restore the lotus-wealth of the waters,
whose lotuses had been destroyed by the frost.
Subsisting on only self-fallen dry leaves of trees
was indeed the utmost limit of austerity; but she, further,

children.text: parā hi kāṣṭhā tapasas tayā punaḥ
children.translated_text: even that set aside — therefore those who know ancient lore
call the sweet-spoken one '<s>Aparṇā</s>' (without a leaf).
Thus, with vows like these that caused her body,
tender as a lotus stalk, to waste away day and night,
she far surpassed the austerities
earned by ascetics with hardened bodies.
Then there entered the grove of austerities a certain <s>jaṭila</s> (matted-hair ascetic),
wearing a deerskin and bark, bold of speech,
blazing as it were with the radiance of <s>Brahman</s>,
like the first stage of life (<s>brahmacarya</s>) embodied.
Him, <s>Pārvatī</s>, as hostess, received
with hospitality preceded by great respect;
for even among those of equal standing and settled mind,
actions of great reverence arise toward those of distinguished appearance.
Having accepted the hospitality duly offered
and having rested a moment, putting aside fatigue,
he, looking at <s>Umā</s> with a straightforward gaze,
began to speak, maintaining proper order:
'Are the <s>samidh</s> (sacrificial fuel) and <s>kuśa</s> grass easily available for the rites?
Are the waters fit for the bathing ritual?
Are you performing your austerities according to your own capacity?
For the body is indeed the primary instrument of <s>dharma</s> (virtue).'
'Do the shoots of these creepers, nourished
by the water you have poured,
rival your lip-cloth
that is pale-red from the lac-dye long since abandoned?'
'Is your mind at peace toward the deer
who steal the <s>darbha</s> grass held in your hand,
and who, O lotus-eyed one, with their restless eyes
seem to imitate the likeness of your own eyes?'
'What is said, O <s>Pārvatī</s>, that beauty does not serve sinful conduct —
that saying is without exception,

children.text: na rūpam ity avyabhicāri tad vacaḥ
children.translated_text: for indeed your character, O one of noble appearance,
has become a model even for ascetics.'
'Not so much by the waters of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> fallen from heaven,
which laugh at the scattered offerings of the Seven Sages,

children.text: tathā na gāṅgaiḥ salilair divaś cyutaiḥ
children.translated_text: as by your stainless conduct
has this mountain-lord been purified along with his lineage.'
'By this [conduct], <s>dharma</s> appears to me today with special distinction,
as the essence of the three goals of life, O blessed one,
since you, whose mind is free from desire for objects and pleasure,
serve <s>dharma</s> alone, having chosen it exclusively.'
'You should not regard me as merely someone
who has been shown special hospitality by you,
Since the meeting of virtuous ones, O one of bowed limbs,
is called by the wise a bond of seven steps.
Therefore, this person, with restlessness natural to a brāhmaṇa,
wishes to ask you, O greatly forbearing one,
something, O lady rich in austerities —
if it is not a secret, please answer.
Birth in the family of the first Creator,
a form as if the beauty of the three worlds had risen,
the happiness of sovereignty unsought, the freshness of youth —

children.text: tapaḥphalaṃ syāt kim ataḥ paraṃ vada
children.translated_text: tell me, what fruit of <s>tapas</s> (austerity) could be beyond this?
Even from unbearable and unwanted circumstances,
such resolve is indeed found in women of spirit.
But with a mind directed along the path of deliberation,

children.text: na dṛśyate tac ca kṛśodari tvayi
children.translated_text: that resolve, O slender-waisted one, is not seen in you.
This form should not be overcome by grief over the unattainable;
O fair-browed one, whence could there be disrespect in your father's house?
There is no violation of your person — who would extend a hand
toward one who is a jeweled hood of serpents?
Why have you cast aside ornaments in your youth
and donned bark-garments that befit old age?
Tell me — if, at evening when moon and stars shine bright,
the night should serve the purpose of dawn.
If you seek heaven, the effort is in vain —
the regions of your father are the realms of the gods.
And if it is a suitor, enough with meditation —

children.text: na ratnam anviṣyati mṛgyate hi tat
children.translated_text: a jewel does not seek a buyer; rather, it is sought.
Your warm sighing has revealed something,

children.text: manas tu me saṃśayam eva gāhate
children.translated_text: yet my mind still plunges into doubt.
No object worthy of your desire is seen
that could possibly be difficult to obtain for one who desires it.
Ah, how steadfast must be the young man you desire,
who, while your ear has long been empty of its lotus-ornament,
disregards the matted locks hanging loosely
on your cheeks, tipped with the tawny hue of young rice.
Seeing you, emaciated beyond measure by ascetic vows,
your ornament-seats scorched by the sun,
like a crescent moon seen during the day —
whose heart among the feeling would not ache?
I know your beloved, deceived by the pride of beauty,
who, of sidelong glances,
long makes an object of those eyes
but not his own face with its curved lashes.
How long will you toil, O <s>Gaurī</s>? There exists
for me too <s>tapas</s> accumulated from a previous birth.
With half of it, obtain your desired

children.text: varaṃ tam icchāmi ca sādhu veditum
children.translated_text: boon — and I wish to know that boon properly.
Thus addressed by the twice-born who had entered,
she was unable to declare what was in her heart.
Then she looked at her companion standing beside her
with eyes turned aside, their collyrium unfaded.
Her friend addressed that brāhmaṇa student:
'Hear, O virtuous one, if you have curiosity —
for what purpose this body, like a lotus warding off heat,
has been made an instrument of <s>tapas</s> by her.'
'This proud one, scorning the lords of the four quarters
beginning with great <s>Indra</s>, who are surpassing in splendor,
through the conquest of <s>Madana</s> (Love) who is irresistible by beauty,
wishes to obtain the <s>Pināka</s>-bearing one (<s>Śiva</s>) as her husband.'
'He, <s>Kāma</s>, the arrow, turned back formerly by the unbearable roar of <s>Śiva</s>,
without reaching the face of the enemy of the cities (<s>Śiva</s>),
pierced this one in the heart with a long-drawn shot —
even though the flower-bowed one (<s>Kāma</s>) had his body shattered.'
'Since then, maddened, in her father's house,
with locks dusted grey from the sandal-paste forehead mark,

children.text: na jātu bālā labhate sma nirvṛtiṃ
children.translated_text: the young girl never found peace
even upon the stone slabs of massed snow.'
'When the deeds of the <s>Pināka</s>-bearer were recounted in colorful narrative,
with words faltering from a tearful throat, she
many a time made weep the daughters of the <s>Kinnara</s>-king,
her companions in song at the edge of the forest.'
'And in the nights with but a third part remaining, for a moment
she closed her eyes and suddenly awoke,
saying in an indistinct voice, "Where are you going, O <s>Nīlakaṇṭha</s> (Blue-throated one)?"
with her arms clasped around a neck that was not there.'
'Since you, who are called by the wise all-pervading,

children.text: na vetsi bhāvastham imaṃ janaṃ katham
children.translated_text: how is it you do not know this person who dwells in your heart?' —
thus, in private, <s>Candraśekhara</s> (the moon-crested one, <s>Śiva</s>)
was reproached by the innocent girl through her own hand-drawn image of him.'
'And when, reflecting on how to attain that Lord of the universe,
she could see no other means,
then with us and with the permission of her guru,
she entered this ascetic grove for <s>tapas</s>.'
'Even in these trees planted by her own hand,
which are themselves witnesses to her austerities, fruit has been seen;
but no sign of approaching fulfillment is visible
for her heart's desire that depends on the moon-crested one.'
'I do not know when that difficult-to-attain one
will approach this friend,
looked upon with tears by her companions, emaciated by <s>tapas</s>,
like a bull approaching a furrow wounded by drought.'
Thus informed by her friend, who knew the signs
and whose true feelings were unconcealed, about the one supremely beautiful in his steadfastness,
he, with signs of joy not yet manifest, asked <s>Umā</s>:
"Is this really so, or a jest?"
Then, placing the crystal rosary
in his outstretched hand with fingers curled,
the daughter of the mountain, with measured words,
spoke — she whose speech had been long held in check.
"As you have heard, O best among knowers of the <s>Vedas</s>,
this person is eager to attain the highest station.
This <s>tapas</s>, they say, is the means to attain that —
there is no path unreachable for desires."
Then the brāhmaṇa student said: "<s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord) is known to me;
you persist in desiring him."
"Considering his fondness for inauspicious practices,
I cannot bring myself to support your pursuit."
"You who are stubbornly set on an unworthy object, how indeed
will this hand of yours, adorned with wedding ornaments,
endure its first contact with <s>Śambhu's</s> hand,
encircled by a serpent as a bracelet?"
"Consider for yourself just this much —

children.text: kadā cid ete yadi yogam arhataḥ
children.translated_text: whether these can ever be a fit pair:"
"a bridal garment marked with the auspicious goose-pattern,
and an elephant-hide dripping with drops of blood."
"Who else, even a stranger, would approve for your feet,
scattered as they are with flowers of the wedding pavilion,
steps marked with lac dye, placed upon
cremation grounds strewn with disheveled hair?"
"What greater incongruity can you speak of than this —
that the breast of the three-eyed one, which is easily yours too,
upon these two breasts, the abode of yellow sandalwood,
the dust of cremation ashes will make its mark?"
"And this is another mockery before you —
that when you, worthy of being carried by a lordly elephant,
are seen riding upon an aged bull,
the great world will be smiling."
"Two things have now become pitiable
because of your desire for union with the skull-bearer —
the beautiful digit of the moon of the graceful crescent-wearer,
and you, the moonlight for the eyes of this world."
"A deformed body, an unascertainable birth,
nudity revealing the absence of wealth —
what is sought in a husband, O girl of fawn-like eyes,

children.text: tad asti kiṃ vyastam api trilocane
children.translated_text: does any of that exist, even scattered, in the three-eyed one?"
"Turn your mind away from this unworthy desire —

children.text: kva tadvidhas tvaṃ kva ca puṇyalakṣaṇā
children.translated_text: where is one like him, and where are you, of auspicious marks?
The Vedic ritual honor of a sacrificial post
is not expected by the wise for a cremation-ground stake."
When the twice-born spoke thus adversely,
with anger discernible in her trembling lower lip,
she fixed upon him her eyes
with furrowed brows, red at the corners.
And she said to him: "You surely do not know <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) in truth,

children.text: na vetsi nūnaṃ yata evam āttha mām
children.translated_text: since you speak thus to me."
"The conduct of great souls, uncommon to the world
and born of inconceivable causes, is reviled by the dull-witted."
"Auspicious rites are practiced by one intent on averting misfortune,
or by one eager for prosperity."
"For him who is the refuge of the world, who is free from desires,
what use are these practices that afflict one's conduct with worldly hopes?"
"Having nothing, he is the source of all wealth;
the Lord of the three worlds, he frequents the abode of the departed."
"He of terrifying form is called <s>Śiva</s> (the Auspicious) —
there are none who know the true meaning of the <s>Pināka</s>-bearer."
"Whether adorned with ornaments, with a bound serpent,
or wearing an elephant-hide, or clad in fine cloth,"
"whether bearing a skull, or crescent-crowned —
the form of him whose body is the universe cannot be determined."
"Having attained contact with his limbs,
cremation-ash surely becomes a means of purification."
"For thus, that which falls during the performance of his dance,
is smeared upon their heads by the celestial beings."
"His impoverished state, as he rides upon a bull? —
The bull that is the mount of the rut-streaming lord of elephants of the directions"
performs obeisance at his feet with its crown,
its toes reddened with the pollen of the ever-wakeful <s>Mandāra</s> flowers.
"Even while intending to speak of faults, yet fallen from yourself,
you have spoken one thing truly about the Lord —"
"He whom even the self-born ones (<s>Brahmā</s> and others) celebrate as the Cause —
how can he be one whose origin is ascertainable?"
"Enough of argument! As you have heard him described,
let him be entirely of that nature."
"My mind is fixed, of one essence with love —
desire does not regard what is to be said about its object."

children.text: nivāryatām āli kim apy ayaṃ baṭuḥ
children.translated_text: "Restrain this young student, O friend, who is about to speak again,
his lower lip quivering with eagerness."
"Not only one who reviles the great is a sinner,

children.text: śṛṇoti tasmād api yaḥ sa pāpabhāk
children.translated_text: but also one who listens — that one too partakes of sin."
Saying "I shall go from here," the young maiden
moved, her bark-garment parted by her breasts.
Then, assuming his true form, with a smile,
the one whose banner bears the bull (<s>Śiva</s>) clasped her.
Seeing him, she trembled, her tender body moist with emotion,
bearing a foot raised but unable to set it down,
like a river confused by the shifting of mountains in its path —
the daughter of the king of mountains neither went nor stood.
"From this day forth, O one with bowed limbs, I am your servant,
purchased by your austerities" — when the moon-crested one said this,
she at once released the fatigue born of her vows.

children.text: kleśaḥ phalena hi punar navatāṃ vidhatte
children.translated_text: For toil, when bearing fruit, takes on newness once again.
Then <s>Gaurī</s> sent through a friend
a private message to the Soul of the Universe:
"The lord of mountains is my giver in marriage —
let him be made the authority."
Having uttered the message through her,
she shone, quiet in the presence of her beloved,
like a mango shoot nearby,
voiced by the <s>kokilā</s> (cuckoo) in spring.
He, having agreed "so be it,"
and having somehow let <s>Umā</s> depart,
the chastiser of <s>Smara</s> (Love) recalled
the seven sages made of light.
Those rich in <s>tapas</s>, illuminating the sky
with their circles of radiance,
accompanied by <s>Arundhatī</s>, appeared instantly
before the Lord.
They who had bathed in the streams of the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s>,
in waves scattered with flowers of the bank-side <s>Mandāra</s> trees,
fragrant with the ichor
of the elephants of the directions.
Wearing pearl sacred threads,
clad in golden bark,
with jeweled rosaries — as if <s>Kalpavṛkṣa</s> (wish-fulfilling trees)
had taken to the ascetic life.
By the thousand-rayed one (<s>Sūrya</s>, the Sun),
whose horse is driven downward at sunset
and whose banner is drawn in as it sets,
they were ever looked upon with due reverence.
Along with the Earth, held up
by the intertwining of <s>Viṣṇu's</s> arm-creepers,
they rested upon the tusk of the Great Boar (<s>Varāha</s>)
at the time of the cosmic dissolution.
Because of continuing the work of creation
after the universal progenitor,
these ancient ones were celebrated by the knowers of antiquity
as the Creators (<s>Dhātāras</s>).
They were ascetics who enjoyed
the fruits of their ancient, purified
and ripened
austerities.
Among them, the virtuous <s>Arundhatī</s>,
her gaze fixed upon her husband's feet,
shone greatly, as if she were
the embodied perfection of <s>tapas</s>.
The Lord beheld her without distinction of respect
from the sages —
"this one is a woman, this a man" — such disregard does not apply;
for conduct is what is honored among the virtuous.
From seeing them, <s>Śambhu's</s> eagerness
for taking a wife increased further.
For virtuous wives are indeed the root and means
of all righteous actions.
When even by <s>dharma</s> a step was taken
toward <s>Pārvatī</s> on <s>Śarva's</s> (<s>Śiva's</s>) behalf,
the mind of <s>Kāma</s> (Love), fearful of his former offense,
breathed again.
Then all those sages,
having honored the guru of the universe,
the learned ones, with the hair on their bodies standing erect with joy,
spoke thus:
"Whatever <s>Brahman</s> (the Vedas) has been properly recited,
whatever has been duly offered into the fire,
whatever <s>tapas</s> has been performed — of all that,
the ripened fruit is for us today."
"That you, the overseer of the worlds,
have elevated us,
raising us beyond the domain of desire
to the domain of your own mind."
"He in whose mind you would dwell
is already the best among the accomplished."
"What then of one who, born of <s>Brahmā</s>,
dwells in your mind?"
"Truly, we occupy a station beyond
the sun and the moon."
"But today, higher even than that,
we have risen by your grace of remembering us."
"We esteem ourselves greatly
because we are honored by you."
"For the highest regard mostly produces confidence
in one's own virtues."
"The joy, O <s>Virūpākṣa</s> (Odd-eyed one),
born of meditating upon you —"
"why should that be reported to you?
You are the inner self of all embodied beings."
"We have seen you directly, yet
we do not truly know you."
Be gracious, tell us about yourself;
you do not move within the path of [our] intellects.
Are you the one by whom you create the manifest [world],
or the one by whom you sustain it?
Or are you the destroyer of the universe?
Which portion is this of yours?
Or rather, O God, let this
very great request remain [as it is];
command us, meanwhile, who have arrived with a purpose in mind —
what shall we do?
Then, with the clear rays of his teeth,
supplementing the light of the moon perched upon his crest,
gathering up a slender radiance,
the Supreme Lord replied:
'It is known to you that none of my
activities are for my own sake;
have I not been indicated as such
by my eight forms?'
'I, by the gods oppressed by their enemy,
tormented with thirst, like <s>cātaka</s> birds [begging] for rain
from a cloud bearing lightning,
have been asked for an offspring.'
'Therefore I wish to take
<s>Pārvatī</s> for the sake of [my] begetting a son,
like a sacrificer [takes] the fire-churning stick
for the production of the fire that consumes the oblation.'
'<s>Himālaya</s> should be asked by you on my behalf
for her [hand];
for alliances properly entered into
do not lend themselves to alteration.'
'With him who is lofty, steadfast,
who bears the burden of the earth —
know me too as one whose alliance with him
is without deception.'
'Thus should he be addressed for [the purpose of obtaining] the maiden;
how [exactly to speak] is not prescribed by me to you,
for the virtuous follow
the conduct established by you.'
'The noble <s>Arundhatī</s> too
ought to take part in this matter,
for generally in affairs of this kind
married women show boldness.'
'Go then to <s>Oṣadhiprastha</s>,
the city of <s>Himavat</s>, for the accomplishment [of this],
and at this waterfall of the <s>Mahākośī</s> [river]
shall be our meeting again.'
When he, the foremost of the self-controlled,
became inclined toward marriage,
the ascetics descended from <s>Prajāpati</s>
abandoned their embarrassment about possessions.
Then, having said 'Very well,' the assembly of sages
set forth,
and the Blessed One too arrived
at the place first designated [by him].
Those supreme sages, rising into the dark-blue sky,
equal in speed to thought,
reached <s>Oṣadhiprastha</s>,
[passing through the sky] without lingering.
Surpassing <s>Alakā</s> itself,
the abode of abundant wealth,
[the city appeared] as if made to accommodate
the overflow of heaven.
Encircled by the streams of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> as its moat,
with luminous herbs blazing within its ramparts,
with great halls of gem-stones —
captivating even when guarded.
Where the elephants had conquered the fear of lions,
where the horses were born from underground [caverns],
where <s>Yakṣas</s> and <s>Kiṃpuruṣas</s> were the citizens,
and forest-goddesses were the women.
Where, in the mansions to whose peaks clouds clung,
the sounds of <s>muraja</s> drums made through instruments
seemed doubtful — [whether they were the drums]
or the accompanying thunder [of the clouds].
Where, by the wish-fulfilling trees alone,
with their waving branch-garments,
the beauty of flags upon the houses' pole-mechanisms
was produced without human effort.
Where, in the crystal palaces,
at night, in the banquet halls,
the reflections of the stars
served as offerings.
Where, by the light of the [luminous] herbs,
their paths lit up at night,
the women going to secret assignations (<s>abhisārikā</s>)
were unacquainted with darkness, even on cloudy days.
Where old age extended only to the end of youth;
affliction was [only] the flower-armed [god of love];
sleep arose only from the weariness of love;
and loss of consciousness was [only] a misnomer.
Where, by [their] frowning brows, trembling lips,
and graceful threatening with the finger,
the [feigned] angers of the women
made their lovers supplicants for reconciliation.
And whose outer garden,
shaded by <s>Saṃtānaka</s> trees, where <s>Vidyādhara</s> travelers slept,
was the fragrant
<s>Gandhamādana</s> [mountain] itself.
Then those divine sages,
seeing the city of the <s>Himālaya</s>,
considered it a deception — merit performed
with an eye toward heaven [yet yielding something better].
They descended swiftly at the palace of the mountain,
gazed upon with upturned faces by the doorkeepers,
with their burdens of matted hair
as motionless as painted fire.
Having descended from the sky,
with the eldest at the front as is proper,
that succession of sages shone
like a row of stars [reflected] within water.
Taking the <s>arghya</s> (honorific offering) for those worthy of <s>arghya</s>,
the mountain came forth to meet them from afar,
bending the earth
with the weight of his heavy footsteps.
Tall, with lips reddened by mineral pigment,
with broad arms [like] <s>devadāru</s> (deodar) cedars,
with a chest of rock by his very nature —
clearly [identified as] <s>Himavān</s>.
Showing the way himself,
with honors rendered according to prescribed rites,
he had those of pure conduct
enter his inner apartments.
There, when those lords had seated themselves on wicker seats
and he had taken his own seat,
the mountain-bearer, with folded hands,
spoke these words:
'Rain without a preceding cloud;
fruit without a visible blossom;
your visit appears to me
as something arrived unexpectedly.'
'I consider myself, by your grace,
as one who was ignorant and has become enlightened,
as iron that has become gold,
as one who has risen from earth to heaven.'
'From this day forth, I am accessible
to beings for purification,
for that which is occupied by the venerable
is declared to be a holy place.'
'I know myself to be purified
by two things, O best of the twice-born:
by the fall of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> upon my head,
and by the water that has washed your feet.'
'My moving [part] is in the status of your servant;
my stationary [part] is marked by your feet;
I consider my body, though of two forms,
to have received your grace in both divisions.'
'The delight that swells from your honoring me
grows [so great] that
even my limbs, though extending to the ends of the directions,
are insufficient for it.'
'Not only the darkness residing in my caves,
but by the sight of you, O luminous ones,
the inner darkness beyond
<s>rajas</s> (passion) too has been dispelled from me.'
'I do not see what task you have [here];
if there were one, what would be impossible?
I suspect your journey here
was merely for my purification.'
'Nevertheless, please deign to give me
some command,
for servants take delight
in being employed by the powerful.'
'Here we are, here is my wife,
this maiden is the life of our family;
tell us where your business lies among these —
we have no attachment to external things.'
Having spoken thus, <s>Himālaya</s>
with the echo spreading from the mouths of caves,
as it were spoke that same message
a second time.
Then the sages prompted <s>Aṅgiras</s>,
the foremost in the matter of illustration,
and he addressed
the mountain-bearer in reply:
'All this is befitting,
and even more than this, in you;
of your mind and of your peaks
the loftiness is the same.'
'Rightly do they call you, the mountain-souled,
<s>Viṣṇu</s>; for indeed your womb
has come to be the support
of all beings, moving and stationary.'
'How would the <s>Nāga</s> (serpent) have borne the earth
with his hoods soft as lotus stalks,
had you not supported [it]
from the depths down to the underworld?'
'Unbroken, stainless, of continuous flow,
unobstructed by ocean waves —
your fame and your rivers
purify the worlds by their sanctity.'
'Just as the <s>Gaṅgā</s> is praised
for [originating from] the foot of the Supreme Being (<s>Parameṣṭhin</s>),
so too is she praised for her second origin —
from your lofty head.'
'The greatness of <s>Hari</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), when he raised [his foot in the] three strides,
pervaded in all directions — across, above, and below;
and that [same all-pervading greatness]
is natural to you.'
'By you, who have taken your place among
those who partake of sacrificial shares,
the lofty golden peak
of <s>Meru</s> has been rendered insignificant.'
'All the hardness in an immovable body
has been deposited in you;
but this body of yours, bowed with devotion,
is [the means of] propitiating the virtuous.'
'Now hear the purpose of our coming —
it is in fact your own business;
but through the instruction of what is auspicious,
we have a share in it.'
'He who, endowed with the powers beginning with <s>aṇimā</s> (minuteness),
unsurpassed by any person,
bears aloft the designation "Lord" (<s>Īśvara</s>)',
along with the half-moon [on his crest];
'By whom this universe is sustained within himself,
through elements beginning with earth, arranged with mutually assigned powers,
like a chariot on a road
by its yoke-animals;'
'Whom <s>yogins</s> seek,
dwelling within the field [of the body],
whose state the wise declare
to be free from the fear of return;'
'He, <s>Śambhu</s>, the granter of boons, the direct witness
of the world's actions,
chooses your daughter,
through words conveyed by us.'
'You should unite her, like meaning
with [the goddess of] speech, with your daughter;
for a father's daughter is beyond sorrow
when given to a worthy husband.'
'As long as these beings exist,
both stationary and moving,
they will regard her as their mother —
