for the Lord is the father of the world.'
'Having bowed to the blue-throated one (<s>Śiva</s>),
the gods thereafter
will redden her feet
with the rays of their crest-jewels.'
'<s>Umā</s> is the bride, you are the giver,
we are the suitors;
the bridegroom is <s>Śambhu</s> — surely this arrangement
suffices for the exaltation of your lineage.'
'Of him who is unpraised yet is praised,
who is worthy of homage yet bows to no other —
through the rite of [giving] a daughter's [hand],
become the <s>guru</s> (elder) of the world's <s>guru</s>.'
While the divine sage spoke thus,
<s>Pārvatī</s>, at her father's side, with downcast face,
was counting
the petals of a play-lotus.
The mountain, though his desire was fully satisfied,
looked toward the face of <s>Menā</s>;
for generally, in the matter of a daughter,
householders have their eyes upon their wives.
<s>Menā</s> too considered all that
to be her husband's desired undertaking;
for devoted wives are unwavering
in what their husband desires.
Having reflected with his mind
'this is the proper answer here,'
at the conclusion of [the sage's] words, he took his daughter
adorned with auspicious ornaments.
'Come, dear child, you have been prepared
as an alms-gift for the Soul of the universe;
the sages have come seeking — the fruit
of being a householder has been attained by me.'
Having said this much to his daughter,
the mountain said to the sages:
'She bows to all of you —
the bride of the three-eyed one.'
They, applauding the mountain's words,
generous in the fulfillment of the desired aim,
nurtured <s>Ambikā</s> with blessings
that bore fruit immediately.
Her, whose golden ear-ornament had slipped
from the earnestness of her bow,
<s>Arundhatī</s> lifted
onto her lap, as she stood blushing.
And her mother, tear-faced,
distraught with love for her daughter —
[<s>Arundhatī</s>] comforted her with the virtues
of the bridegroom who had had no other [wife] before.
Asked about the wedding date
by that kinsman of <s>Hara</s> [i.e., <s>Himālaya</s>], at that very moment,
they, announcing [it as] three days hence,
departed, wearing their bark-garments.
They, having taken leave of <s>Himālaya</s>,
having looked once more upon the trident-bearer (<s>Śiva</s>),
and having reported to him the accomplished purpose,
dismissed by him, rose into the sky.
<s>Paśupati</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) too passed those days with difficulty,
eager for the meeting with the mountain's daughter;
what other helpless being would not be unsettled by

children.text: vibhum api taṃ yad amī spṛśanti bhāvāḥ
children.translated_text: these emotions that touch even the all-powerful lord?
Then, at the auspicious moment when the Lord of herbs [the Moon] was waxing,
on a date endowed with the qualities befitting a son-in-law,
<s>Himavān</s>, with his kinsmen assembled,
undertook the rites of the wedding consecration for his daughter.
With nuptial festive preparations
and groups of busy married women in every house,
the city of the mountain, out of affection,
together with the inner apartments, seemed like a single family.
Its great thoroughfare, strewn with <s>Saṃtānaka</s> flowers,
with a row of banners fashioned from Chinese silk,
blazing with the luster of golden arches,
shone like a heaven in another place.
Even though there was a line of sons, <s>Umā</s> alone,
as one seen after a long time, as one risen from the dead,
with her wedding ceremony at hand,
became a special cause of joy for her parents.
She passed from lap to lap, showered with blessings;
she received ornament after ornament;
the affection of the mountain's family, though divided among relatives,
found its sole resting place in her.
At the auspicious hour when the moon
had conjoined with the asterism <s>Uttaraphalgunī</s>,
the kinswomen who were blessed with husbands and sons
performed the beautifying rites upon her body.
She adorned herself with the anointing-attire —
of a garment of fine silk free from the navel-knot, with an arrow [of Love] placed [upon it],
with shoots of <s>dūrvā</s> grass interspersed with its varied hue
like white mustard seeds and other auspicious items.
And the maiden shone, having come into contact
with the new arrow of the wedding consecration-rite,
like the crescent of the moon being kindled
by the hand of the sun at the end of the dark fortnight.
Her, with body-oil removed by a paste of <s>lodhra</s>,
with body-paint made of dried <s>kāleyaka</s> (sandalwood),
wearing a garment fit for the ablution —
the women led her toward the nuptial pavilion.
On this [platform] set with <s>vaidūrya</s> (cat's-eye) stone tiles,
decorated with patterns of inlaid pearls,
with water poured from eight golden pitchers,
they bathed her to the accompaniment of music.
She, with limbs purified by the auspicious bath,
having put on a garment fit for the bridegroom's approach,
shone like the earth after the ablution of rainwater
has concluded, with <s>kāśa</s> grass in full bloom.
From that spot, the faithful wives led her,
taking hold [of her], to the center of the nuptial altar,
which was canopied, supported by four pillars of gems,
with a prepared seat.
Having seated that slender one there, facing east,
those seated before her paused for a moment.
their eyes drawn away by the beauty of the real thing,
even though the toilette was at hand.
Her hair, freed of its dampness
by the warmth of incense, with a flower placed within,
one [attendant] wrapped it in a noble coiffure
with a pale <s>madhūka</s>-flower garland entwined with <s>dūrvā</s> grass.
They applied white <s>aguru</s> (aloe paste) and made upon her body
a design of <s>gorocanā</s> (yellow orpiment) leaf-patterns;
she stood surpassing the beauty
of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> with its sandbanks marked by <s>cakravāka</s> birds.
The beauty of her face, with its celebrated locks,
surpassing the lotus with clinging bees
and the moon's orb with its streak of cloud,
cut short any occasion for comparison.
On her cheek — roughened by the astringent <s>lodhra</s> paste,
delicately pale at the edges from a touch of <s>gorocanā</s> —
a sprout of barley, placed at the ear,
captivated the eyes by gaining supreme beauty there.
And the lower lip of that well-proportioned woman, divided by a line,
its hue slightly polished with beeswax,
quivering, enhanced an indescribable beauty,
like fruit ripe with imminent loveliness.
'Touch with this the crescent moon on your husband's head!' —
at this jest from a friend,
she, having dyed [her friend's] feet with lac, [and] offering a blessing,
struck her with a garland, leaving her speechless.
Looking at her eyes, beautiful as the petals of a fine blue lotus,
the attendants, upon examination,
with the awareness of a special luster in the eyes,
applied black collyrium only as an auspicious rite.
She, having her ornaments put on, shone
like a creeper with blossoming flowers,
like a night with rising stars,
like a river with alighting birds.
And beholding her own beauty shining
in the mirror's image, with motionless wide eyes,
she became eager for the approach of <s>Hara</s> (Śiva) —
for the toilette of women has its fruit in being seen by the beloved.
Then her mother, taking with her fingers
moist yellow orpiment, the auspicious <s>manaḥśilā</s> (realgar),
and a spotless tooth-pick of leaf placed at the ear,
lifted her daughter's face upward.
The very first wish that had arisen
and grown along with the budding of <s>Umā</s>'s breasts,
<s>Menā</s> somehow made that same wish of her daughter
into the <s>tilaka</s>-mark of the wedding consecration.
And with tear-blurred vision, she tied upon her [daughter]
the woolen auspicious wedding-thread for the hand,
arranged in a new position,
being slipped on by the fingers of the nurse.
Like the shore of the Milk Ocean with heaps of foam,
like an autumn night with a full moon,
she, wearing a new, fresh linen garment,
shone even more, holding up a mirror.
Her mother, having made her bow to the family deities
who had been worshipped, and to the eldest women of the family,
skilled in directing what was to be done,
had her touch the feet of the virtuous women in order.
'May you obtain undivided love from your husband' —

children.text: ity ucyate tābhir umā sma namrā
children.translated_text: thus blessed by them, <s>Umā</s> bowed her head;
but by her, who would share half the body of that [lord],
even the blessings of her affectionate relatives were surpassed.
The mountain, having completed in full all that was fitting
in accordance with his wish and his prosperity for her,
stood in the assembly hall where well-wishers were gathered,
awaiting the arrival of the one marked by the bull.
Meanwhile, on <s>Kubera</s>'s mountain too, the adornment for the groom,
suitable for his first taking of the hand [in marriage],
was placed before the Chastiser of Cities (<s>Śiva</s>)
by the doting <s>Mātṛs</s> (divine mothers).
The beauty of the auspicious wedding ornaments
was merely touched by the Lord, out of respect for it;
his own usual attire, for the bridegroom,
assumed a different, desired aspect by the power of that great lord.
The very ashes became white body-ointment;
the skull itself became the beauty of a spotless crest-jewel;
and the <s>gorocanā</s>-mark at the edges
was the very elephant-hide assuming the nature of silk.
The eye that gleamed between the skull-halves,
with a pure tawny pupil set within,
in the presence [of the orpiment],
itself served as the <s>tilaka</s>-mark application.
As the lord-serpents on each appropriate [part of the body]
were about to assume the status of other ornaments,
only their bodies underwent transformation,
while the splendor of their hood-jewels remained as it was.
Since the crescent moon, even by day, emitting rays of light,
with its mark not yet revealed due to its youth,
always adorned the crown of <s>Hara</s> whose crest is ever broken [by it],
what need was there for a crest-jewel?
Thus the Creator, the sole source of wonders,
by his own power, the author of the well-known art of costume,
beheld his own reflection in a sword
brought near by a <s>gaṇa</s> attendant.
He, leaning on <s>Nandī</s>'s arm, mounted
the bull, whose broad back was covered with a tiger skin,
its great size reduced by devotion to him,
and set forth as if ascending <s>Kailāsa</s> itself.
The <s>Mātṛs</s> (divine mothers), following the god,
their ornaments swaying from the jolting of their mounts,
with their faces pale with the dust of the halo of light,
made the sky as if it were a lotus pond.
Behind those golden-hued ones,
<s>Kālī</s>, adorned with skulls, shone
like a dark row of rain-clouds with herons,
with lightning cast far ahead.
Then the sound of auspicious trumpets,
raised by the <s>gaṇas</s> preceding the Trident-bearer,
penetrating the pinnacles of aerial palaces,
announced to the gods the occasion for attendance.
The thousand-rayed one (<s>Sūrya</s>) took up for him
a new parasol fashioned by <s>Tvaṣṭṛ</s>;
he, his crown not far from that silk [canopy],
shone as if with the <s>Gaṅgā</s> falling upon his head.
Then the <s>Gaṅgā</s> and the <s>Yamunā</s> in embodied form
attended the god with fly-whisks;
even though the ocean and the river were reversed [in position],
they appeared as if with their swans alighting.
First <s>Brahmā</s> followed him,
and the Person himself, marked with the <s>Śrīvatsa</s>;
with the word 'Victory!' which augmented his greatness
like an oblation [feeding] fire.
That single form divided itself into three;
their common nature, and their primacy and subsequence:
<s>Viṣṇu</s> is sometimes <s>Hara</s>, and <s>Hari</s> is his,

children.text: vedhās tayos tāv api dhātur ādyau
children.translated_text: and <s>Brahmā</s> is of those two, yet those two are also the Creator's first.
The world-guardians, led by <s>Puruhūta</s> (<s>Indra</s>),
their attire humbled by the surrender of their auspicious insignia,
at the signal of <s>Nandī</s> for the granting of an audience,
shown [into his presence], bowed with joined palms.
With a nod of the head he honored the Lotus-born (<s>Brahmā</s>),
with a word [he honored] <s>Hari</s>, with a smile the slayer of <s>Vṛtra</s> (<s>Indra</s>),
and with a mere glance all the other gods —
each according to his rank.
The Seven Sages offered him a benediction of victory before [all];
he addressed them with a smile:
'At this wedding sacrifice that is being performed,
you are the officiating priests, previously chosen by me.'
With his exploits of [destroying] the three cities being sung
by skilled [musicians] led by <s>Viśvāvasu</s>,
the bearer of the crescent moon traversed the road,
surpassing the disturbances of the darkness of the way.
His mount, moving through the sky,
with tinkling golden bells,
shaking repeatedly the horns on which thick [clouds] were impaled,
as if [clearing] mud stuck [on them] from striking the banks.
He reached in an instant the city guarded by the king of mountains,
never before assailed by an enemy,
as though drawn forward
by <s>Hara</s>'s glances clinging to the city like golden threads.
Near it, the dark-throated god,
gazed at with upturned faces by the curious citizens,
descending from his own arrow-marked path [in the sky],
approached near to the surface of the earth.
The mountain-king, confirmed of his arrival,
came forth to meet him with herds of elephants
mounted by his wealthy kinsmen,
like his own mountain ranges with trees in full bloom.
The two hosts — of the gods and of the mountain [folk] —
at the gate of the city, its doors thrown open,
met, their sounds spreading far,
like two floods of water whose common embankment is broken.
The mountain was abashed at being bowed to
by <s>Hara</s>, who is venerated by the three worlds;

children.text: pūrvaṃ mahimnā sa hi tasya dūram
children.translated_text: for previously, overcome by his [own] greatness,
he had not noticed his own head bowing far [before Śiva].
He, his facial beauty blossoming with joy,
taking the lead before the bridegroom,
ushered him into the splendid palace,
its market-road strewn with flowers up to the ankles.
At that moment, the beautiful women of the city,
eager to behold <s>Īśāna</s> (Śiva),
on the rows of balconies, performed such
actions, abandoning all other tasks:
One, rushing suddenly to the viewing window,
whose garland had come undone from the hurry,
neither greeted her kinsman who arrived just then,
nor caught her mass of hair though restrained by her hand.
Another, snatching away her forefoot that was being held
by the attendant applying liquid lac,
rushed with playful gait to the window
and left a trail of lac-marks in her path.
Having adorned her right eye with collyrium,
cheating her left eye of the same,
another went just as she was to the window's proximity,
still carrying the applicator stick.
Another, sending her gaze through the lattice,
did not tie the girdle-knot loosened by her departure;
with her hand, into which the light of her ornaments had entered [around] the navel,
she stood, holding up her garment.
The girdle of one who had risen in haste
while it was only half-strung, coming undone at every step
in an inauspicious manner,
was reduced to the last thread held at the root of her thumb.
The windows of those women,
filled with intense curiosity,
with their faces fragrant with wine-breath
and their restless-eyed, bee-like glances, were like [lotuses] adorned with thousand petals.
Then the crescent-crowned one entered the royal highway,
festooned with banners, with raised arches,
making even by day the turret-tops
double in splendor as if bathed in moonlight.
Drinking in with their eyes that single sight,
the women did not turn to other objects of sense;
for the activity of their remaining senses
had, as it were, entirely entered into their sight.
'Rightly was the severe penance endured for this purpose
by <s>Aparṇā</s> (Pārvatī), tender as she is;

children.text: yā dāsyam apy asya labheta nārī
children.translated_text: any woman who might obtain even servitude to him
would be fulfilled — how much more the sharing of his couch!'
'If this pair, mutually enhancing each other's beauty,
were not to be joined together,
the effort of the Father of Creatures in designing beauty
for these two would have been in vain.'
'Surely <s>Kāma</s>'s body was not burned
by this one in rising anger;
I think that <s>Kāma</s>, seeing this god,
abandoned his body of his own accord, out of shame.'
'Having obtained this alliance with the Lord
that was desired even in his fondest wishes,
the Mountain King, O friend, will hold
his head, [already] lofty from bearing the earth, even higher!'
Hearing these conversations of the women of <s>Oṣadhiprastha</s> (the Mountain City),
pleasing to the ear, the three-eyed one
reached the abode of <s>Himālaya</s>,
with fistfuls of parched rice ground to powder by [the women's] bracelets.
Alighting there, his hand held by <s>Acyuta</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>),
like the sun from an autumn cloud descending to the cattle,
he entered the inner courtyards of the mountain-lord,
previously trodden by the Lotus-seated (<s>Brahmā</s>).
After him, the gods led by <s>Indra</s>,
and the supreme sages preceded by the Seven Sages,
and the <s>gaṇas</s> approached the mountain's abode,
like noble purposes [approaching] a well-commenced enterprise.
There the Lord, receiving his seat of honor duly,
accepted the <s>arghya</s> (offering) with a jewel, and the honeyed cow-product,
and the new silk garments brought by the mountain —
all except the [Vedic] mantras.
He, clad in silk, was led to the bride's vicinity
by modest harem-guards,
like the ocean with its line of bright foam
approaching the shore with new moonbeams.
Joined with the maiden whose moonlike facial luster had increased,
whose lotus-eyes had blossomed,
<s>Śiva</s>, with his heart's waters clear, became
like the world being touched by autumn.
When they came together, their eyes —
timid, somewhat controlled and withdrawn,
restrained by modesty — at that very moment
became restless toward each other.
The eight-formed one (<s>Śiva</s>) took her hand
with its copper-hued fingers, presented by the mountain-lord —
on <s>Umā</s>'s body, as if a first sprouting
of <s>Smara</s> (Love), who was hidden in his body, and who feared that [hand].
A horripilation appeared on <s>Umā</s>;
the bull-bannered one's fingers perspired;
the effect of their hands' meeting upon those two
seemed as if equally distributed by <s>Manobhava</s> (Love).
When other bride and groom pairs, upon performing the hand-taking,
are endowed with supreme beauty —
what need is there to speak of the beauty of both of these
at that time, by virtue of their proximity?
From the circumambulation of the fire
with rising flames, that couple shone
like day and night, intertwined,
moving near the slopes of <s>Meru</s>.
Having led the bride and groom thrice around the fire,
the officiating priest made the bride, whose eyes closed
at the touch of [his] fingertips,
the offering of parched grain in that fire with blazing flames.
She directed to her face the offering-handful
of smoke from the parched grain, fragrant with the desired scent, as instructed by the preceptor;
that flame, creeping along her cheek,
momentarily attained the beauty of a blue lotus at her ear.
The bride's face became slightly moist with a reddish line on the cheeks,
with the dark collyrium streaked by her sighs at the eyes,
with the barley-ear ornament wilting,
from receiving the smoke as prescribed by custom.
The <s>brāhmaṇa</s> said to the bride: 'This fire, O child,
is the first witness to your marriage;
the practice of <s>dharma</s> with <s>Śiva</s> as your husband
must be performed by you without hesitation.'
Extending her ear to the very end of what was being said,
<s>Bhavānī</s> drank in those words of the preceptor,
like the earth [drinking] the first monsoon rain
of <s>Indra</s>, after the fierce heat of the hot season.
Directed by her husband of firm gaze to look at <s>Dhruva</s> (the Pole Star)
— he whose appearance was itself pleasing —
she, lifting her face and saying 'It is seen,'
spoke somehow, her throat constricted with modesty.
Thus, by the officiating priest who knew the rites,
the ceremony of taking the hand having been duly performed,
those two, the parents of all creatures, bowed
to the Grandfather (<s>Brahmā</s>), seated on a lotus throne.
The bride was congratulated by the Creator: 'May you be
auspicious and the mother of heroes,'
yet he, though being <s>Vācaspati</s> (Lord of Speech) himself, regarding the eight-formed one (<s>Śiva</s>),
having wished [him well], became immersed in anxious thought.
Then, having come to the square altar with its arranged offerings,
the two, seated on golden seats,
underwent the worldly custom that must be observed:
the sprinkling of moist unbroken rice, as husband and wife.
Over them, <s>Lakṣmī</s> held a lotus parasol
with a long stalk,
beautiful with a net of pearls drawn forth
by the clusters of water drops clinging between its petals.
And <s>Sarasvatī</s> blessed that couple with speech
employed in two forms:
the bridegroom — best among the worthy — with words purified by ritual
the bride with words whose import was easy to grasp.
They watched for a moment the first performance
of the <s>Apsarases</s> (celestial nymphs), with graceful gestures,
displaying varied modes of expression at the junctures
and passion fixed in the different <s>rasas</s> (aesthetic sentiments).
At the end of that, the gods, falling down with folded hands
raised to their diadems, before <s>Hara</s> (Śiva) who had taken his bride,
entreated the service of the five-arrowed one (<s>Kāma</s>),
who had regained his body at the end of the curse.
The Blessed One, free from anger, assented to that —
the operation of the arrows even upon himself,
for a petition by those who know the right occasion,
made at the proper time, attains success with masters.
Then the moon-crested one (<s>Śiva</s>), having dismissed those hosts of gods,
taking the mountain-king's daughter by the hand,
went to the nuptial chamber, beautiful with the splendor
of golden vases and red lac, with a couch prepared on the ground.
There, the Lord made <s>Gaurī</s>, adorned with the blush of her new marriage,
who was turning her face away and looking up because of his [teasing] gestures,
though she had given her word to her bed-chamber companions,
laugh secretly at the facial contortions of the <s>Pramathas</s> (Śiva's attendants).
After the ceremony of taking the hand,
the mountain-king's daughter, toward <s>Hara</s>,
from the seizure of emotion and timidity,
acquired a body enchanting with the longings of desire.
When addressed, she gave no answer;
she wished to leave, her garment being held;
she lay on the bed with her face turned away —
yet even so, she served the pleasure of <s>Pinākin</s> (Śiva).
When <s>Pārvatī</s>, who lay in feigned sleep, out of curiosity
opened her eye as [Śiva] gazed directly into her face,
she closed it [at once] when her beloved smiled,
as if struck by lightning.
<s>Śaṅkara</s>'s hand, placed on her navel,
was restrained by her trembling [hand];
but then her silk garment itself
slipped far away, its girdle-knot loosened by her breathing.
'Thus, O friend, put aside your timidity
and attend upon <s>Śaṅkara</s> in private' —
she, bewildered, when her beloved was right before her,
could not remember what her companions had instructed.
Even to begin a conversation on some pretext,
the teaching of <s>Anaṅga</s> (Love) dedicated to the question —
<s>Pārvatī</s>, receiving it with a glance,
gave an answer consisting only of a nod of the head.
When she, stripped of her garment,
covered both eyes of the trident-bearer with her two palms,
she realized that his forehead-eye could see —
and in that private moment, was distressed at her futile effort.
Withholding the gift of her lips in kisses,
her hand clenched tight in his merciless embrace —
the bride's love-play, though it tormented the Lord's desire,
was difficult to requite.
A kiss that left the lip unbruised,
and a nail-mark that left no wound —

children.text: yad rataṃ ca sadayaṃ priyasya tat
children.translated_text: and love-making that was gentle — only these of her beloved
<s>Pārvatī</s> could bear, and nothing else.
When her companions were eager to ask about
the events of the night, at dawn,
she did not quench their curiosity, out of modesty,
yet she hastened in her heart to tell them.
And looking in the mirror that showed the marks of love-making,
seeing the reflection of her lover seated behind her
and then her own reflection,
what [gestures of embarrassment] did she not make, out of shyness!
Seeing her, whose youth had been enjoyed by the blue-throated one,
her mother (<s>Menā</s>) was reassured;
for a young wife, being dear to her husband,
dispels the mother's mental sorrow.
For a few days, somehow,
love-play was managed by her with <s>Sthāṇu</s> (Śiva);
gradually coming to know the flavor of <s>Rati</s> (love),
she shed her disposition of finding love-making painful.
Though her breasts were pressed [against him], she embraced her beloved;
she did not withdraw her lips when he sought them;
and his hand, which had become eager to loosen her girdle —
she restrained it only gently.
Indicated by emotion, without any visible displeasure,
full of tender words, anxious at even a moment's separation —
in only a few days, their love,
rooted and mutually dependent, grew deep.
As the bride was devoted to a husband worthy of her,
so the bridegroom was devoted to her;
for the <s>Jāhnavī</s> (Gaṅgā) never departs from the ocean,
and he too found his sole delight in her voice and face.
Having submitted in private to the tutorship
of <s>Śaṅkara</s>, the instructor in love-play,
the very skill in womanly arts she had learned from him
she offered back as the teacher's fee.
<s>Āmbikā</s> (Pārvatī), her lower lip bitten and released,
with her tender hand waving from the pain,
for a moment soothed [the sting] with the cool
crescent-moon fragment on the trident-bearer's crest.
<s>Śaṅkara</s> too, his forehead-eye soiled
with the powder of her hair-braids scattered by kisses,
presented it to the breeze
carrying the fragrance of <s>Pārvatī</s>'s face, fragrant as a blossoming lotus.
Thus, having indulged the path of sensual pleasure,
favored by <s>Manmatha</s> (Love),
the bull-bannered one (<s>Śiva</s>) dwelt in the abode of the mountain-king
with <s>Umā</s> for a month only.
The Self-born one (<s>Śiva</s>), having sought leave of <s>Himavat</s>,
who was afflicted with grief at the separation from his daughter,
sported here and there, flying about
on <s>Kakudmat</s> (his bull Nandi), of immeasurable speed.
Arriving at <s>Meru</s>, the one whose bull is as swift as wind,
the skillful [Śiva], placing <s>Pārvatī</s>'s breasts before him,
enjoyed beds strewn with pliant golden leaves,
able to withstand the force of love-play.
And on the terraces of <s>Mandara</s>,
where the rocks bore the footprints of <s>Padmanābha</s> (Viṣṇu)
and where fresh drops of nectar had descended,
he dwelt — the bee at the lotus of <s>Pārvatī</s>'s face.
On Mount <s>Ekapiṅgala</s>, the world-teacher,
clasped tightly around the neck by her arms
out of fear from the trumpeting of elephants,
enjoyed the clear moonlight.
Once, on the slopes of <s>Malaya</s>, during their love-play,
the southern wind — fragrant with cloves and saffron
and brushing against sandal creepers —
fanned away his beloved's fatigue, like a flatterer.
<s>Umā</s>, splashed by her beloved with golden lotuses,
her eyes closing from the water thrown by his hand,
plunged into a river in the sky,
with rows of fish forming a repeated girdle [around her].
Adorning her with <s>Pārijāta</s> flowers,
fit for the locks of <s>Pulomā</s>'s daughter (<s>Śacī</s>),
in the <s>Nandana</s> grove, the odd-eyed one (<s>Śiva</s>)
was watched with longing by the divine women for a long time.
Thus, <s>Śaṅkara</s>, having enjoyed both celestial
and earthly pleasures in the company of his beloved,
when the sun was reddening at one time,
entered Mount <s>Gandhamādana</s>.
There, resting on a golden rock-slab,
gazing at the sun visible to the eye [as it set],
he spoke to his consort in <s>dharma</s>,
who rested on his left arm:
'Having transferred the lotus-beauty to your two eyes
whose two outer corners are tinged with red,
as if drawing in the world at its dissolution,
this lord of days gathers in the day.'
'As the sun descends, the waterfalls of your father
with their rays dispersing the mist of spray,
are losing the haloes and rainbows
around them.'
'Of the pair of <s>cakravāka</s> birds in the lake,
who cry out with lotus-pollen staining [their beaks],
turning their necks to each other,
striking each other — their small gap has become a great one.'
'The elephants, leaving their daytime station
fragrant from breaking <s>sallakī</s> branches,
take water for [their] revealed footprints —
water bound with bees on the lotuses.'
'See, O one of measured speech, what has been made by the sun
as it hangs at the edge of the western horizon —
like a bridge of gold with its long reflection
across the waters of the lake.'
'The tusked leaders of the wild-boar herds,
deep-mired, overheated by the sun,
emerge scattering the pool,
as if with lotus-root sprouts bitten and bent in their tusks.'
'This peacock, perched on a treetop,
its disc golden-bright as liquid gold,
seems to drink in the day as it wanes,
O you of ample thighs, [drinking] the heat that passes with it.'
'The sky, its water of sunlight drawn off by the sun,
with darkness advancing from the eastern quarter
as if making it muddy on one side,
shines like a lake with a little [water] remaining.'
'The hermitages, with deer entering the courtyard
and young trees moist from root-watering,
with sacrificial fires being kindled as the fire-offering cows come in,
are bearing their beauty.'
'The lotus, closing its calyx, yet remaining a moment
with a crevice still left open,
seems to be offering its interior
to the bee as a dwelling, with affection.'
'The western quarter, with the sun
whose rays are measurable only at the far end,
shines as if adorned like a maiden
with a <s>bandhujīva</s> (noon-flower) <s>tilaka</s> (forehead-mark).'
'The chariot-companions [of the sun] in thousands,
with voices that charm the hearts of chariot-horses,
praise the sun, encircled with the radiance of fire,
with <s>Sāman</s> hymns, drinking the heat of his rays.'
'This [sun] sets in the great ocean,
depositing the day, with horses whose heads are bowed,
their eyes brushed by ear-whisks,
their manes broken against the yoke.'
'When the sun has set, the sky seems to sleep —
such is the course of great radiance:
that which illuminates as long as it has risen,
having fallen, is meant for the closing [of eyes].'
'The form of the sun, followed even by the twilight,
venerable, has been placed at the peak of the setting mountain;
by whom it was honored at its rising —
how would she not follow him in adversity?'
'The cloud-edges, O one with curling tresses, shine
red, yellow, and tawny —
adorned by this twilight with paint-strokes,
as if saying "you shall see [them]."'
'See the twilight glow, distributed by the sun
on the lion-mane-like crests of the mountains,
on the trees bearing fresh shoots,
and on the mineral-streaked peaks, as if portioned out.'
'O daughter of the mountain-king, these knowers of the rites,
the ascetics, performing the water-offering with pure water,
with reverence recite the secret <s>Brahman</s>
at the twilight juncture, for purification.'
'Therefore, please permit me too
for the observance that is before me;
your circle of friends, skilled in entertainment,
will entertain you, O sweet-voiced one.'
Then, biting her lower lip,
the mountain-king's daughter, feigning displeasure at her husband's words,
spoke without cause to <s>Vijayā</s>,
her companion who was near.
The Lord too, having performed the rite
proper for the close of day, preceded by <s>mantras</s>,
returned to <s>Pārvatī</s>, who was silent from pique,
and spoke to her again, with a smile:
'Let go of this anger, O you who are angry without cause;
it is the twilight to which I bowed, not to another woman.',
'Do you not know your own consort in <s>dharma</s>
to be of the same conduct as the <s>cakravāka</s> bird?'
'That form which was formerly abandoned
by the Self-born (<s>Brahmā</s>) when creating the Fathers, O slender one —
that same [form] now attends the setting and the rising [of the sun];
therefore, O proud one, this is my reverence [for the twilight, not another woman].'
'O mountain-king's daughter, see this [twilight] now,
afflicted by the growth of darkness,
with its row of <s>tamāla</s> trees on one bank —
like a river of mineral pigment flowing on a slope.'
'The other direction bears the sunset glow —
the remnant of sunlight mixed with twilight — like a red streak,
the battlefield-earth, [stained] with blood,
was flung sideways like the disc of the setting [sun].
When the light born at the junction of night and day
is obstructed by <s>Sumeru</s>,
this unbridled pitch darkness
spreads in the quarters, O long-eyed one.
Neither upward is the direction of sight, nor downward,
neither from the sides, nor from the front, nor from behind —
this world, enveloped in a flood of darkness,
exists at night as if in the womb.
What is pure, what is turbid; what is still, what is moving;
what is crooked, and what is endowed with the quality of straightness —
all is made equal by darkness;
alas for the greatness of the wicked, which erases distinctions!
Surely the lord of sacrificers [the sun] is rising
to dispel the nocturnal darkness;
O lotus-faced one, the eastern quarter appears
covered as if with <s>kaitaka</s>-pollen.
The starry night, with the moon
whose form is concealed behind <s>Mandara</s>,
seems like you, met by a dear friend,
about to listen to [whispered] words from behind.
Blocked in its emergence until the end of day,
with a smile like the previously seen slender moonlight,
this disc of the moon rises —
like a secret of the quarters, revealed by night.
Look — with water whose [reflected] image is marked
by the disc [of the moon], lustrous as the fruit of a ripe <s>phalinī</s> plant,
by the moon, with a wide gap [between them],
the pair of <s>cakravāka</s> birds is being mocked.
The fresh rays of the lord of herbs [the moon]
can be cut with the cup-shaped tips of your nails
to fashion an ear-ornament for you —
[they are] soft as the tips of tender grass-blades.
As if gathering the mass of darkness
like hair with its fingers of rays,
the moon seems to kiss the face of night
whose lotus-eyes have become buds.
Look, <s>Pārvatī</s> — with the rays of the new moon,
the sky, its darkness half-dispelled,
appears like lake <s>Mānasa</s>,
sullied by the wallowing of elephants, now clearing.
The moon, having abandoned its reddish hue,
has risen here with a purified disc;
indeed, in those of pure nature,
transformations born from the fault of circumstance do not endure.
On the heights, the moon's radiance rests;
in the hollows, the darkness of night seeks refuge —
surely the course of merit and demerit
has been fashioned by the Creator here in its own likeness.
With water-drops from moonstone
set flowing by the moon's rays, the mountain
awakens at an untimely hour these peacocks
sleeping in the trees of its girdle-zone.
See now, O beautiful one, upon the crests
of the wish-fulfilling trees —
with its flickering rays, the moon appears
as if eager to count the strands of pearl-necklaces.
This moonlight mixed with shadows on the mountain,
with its pattern of elevation and depression,
applied in manifold designs,
shines like the adornment of a rutting elephant.
This lunar flood of radiance,
as if unable to bear the weight, having been breathed in and drunk,
splits the night-lotus from its very root,
releasing the hum of bees.
Look — on the wish-fulfilling tree, by the pure
moonlight that creates doubt about form,
only when the wind stirs, O fierce one,
is the turned garment revealed [as cloth, not light].
It would be possible with these [moonbeams],
pretty with the fallen flowers of trees below,
filtered through the lattice of leaves as shreds of moonlight,
to adorn your locks, lifting them with the fingers.
This moon, O beautiful-faced one, is united
with the conjunction-star that has a trembling disc,
trembling with apprehension —
like a bridegroom with a maiden at a new consecration.
Upon your two cheekbones, fair as split ripe-<s>śara</s>-reed,
gleaming with reflected radiance and serene,
the moonlight seems to climb,
with its gaze fixed on the moon's reflected disc [in your eyes].
Bearing in her own hands
<s>kalpavṛkṣa</s>-honey in vessels of red sun-gems,
the presiding goddess of the <s>Gandhamādana</s> forest
has approached you who stand in composure.
Your face, naturally fragrant with moist filaments [of flowers],
with eyes naturally intoxicated and reddened —
having already obtained a dwelling here,
what further quality will intoxication produce, O playful one?
Or let the company of friends, devotedly respectful,
be served — this [drink] kindles passion;
having spoken thus generously, <s>Śaṅkara</s> [<s>Śiva</s>]
made <s>Ambikā</s> [<s>Pārvatī</s>] drink the beverage.
<s>Pārvatī</s>, from consuming that,
underwent a transformation charming even in the virtuous,
wrought by the workings of inscrutable providence —
like a mango tree attaining the nature of a <s>sahakāra</s> (grafted mango).
At that moment, [their] modesty having been reversed,
passion kindled, the couple about to go to the bedchamber —
the beautiful-faced one became subject
to both the trident-bearer [<s>Śiva</s>] and intoxication.
With rolling eyes, faltering speech,
beads of perspiration, and causeless smiles —
not merely with the face but with the eyes did <s>Īśvara</s> [<s>Śiva</s>]
drink long of <s>Umā</s>'s countenance.
Carrying her, whose girdle of golden coins hung loosely,
difficult to bear with the weight of her hips,
<s>Īśvara</s>, whose majesty was gathered through meditation,
entered the jeweled chamber in secret.
There, upon a couch with a coverlet white as swans,
beautiful to see like the sandy banks of the <s>Jāhnavī</s> [<s>Gaṅgā</s>],
the companion of his beloved lay down —
like the lord of <s>Rohiṇī</s> [the moon] upon an autumn cloud.
That love-play of <s>Pārvatī</s> with <s>Śiva</s> —
with disheveled hair, smeared sandalwood paste, nail-marks
placed in reverse, with jealous [passion],
with loosened girdle-strings — did not [lead to] satiation.
Only, by [<s>Śiva</s>] who was compassionate toward his beloved,
when the rows of stars descended,
was the playful desire to close her eyes
[gently induced], as he held her to his chest.
He awoke, greeted with auspicious songs at dawn
by <s>Kinnara</s>s whose music was suffused
with the <s>mūrcchanā</s> (melodic modulation),
together with pools of golden lotuses — fitting for the wise.
For a moment, the couple with loosened embrace,
their pride [playfully] disturbed —
were attended by breezes from the forest-edges of <s>Gandhamādana</s>
that betrayed the opening of lotuses.
At that moment, <s>Hara</s> [<s>Śiva</s>], his gaze stolen
by the rows of nail-marks at the root of her thigh,
prevented his beloved from tightening
her loosened garment.
He, impassioned, delighted
in gazing upon the face of his beloved —
with eyes reddened from wakefulness, lower lip bruised by deep teeth-marks,
hair disheveled, forehead-mark smudged.
That couch — with coverlet disarranged in folds,
with girdle bunched in the middle, its string loosened,
though the night had passed [leaving it] unstained [by darkness],
was not abandoned by them — [still] marked with the red lac from their feet.
He, wishing to enjoy the taste of his beloved's lips
day and night, which produced ever-increasing joy,
reached a state of invisibility to those eager to see him —
because of [not caring for] the announcement of victory [from the battlefield].
With days and nights equal for <s>Śambhu</s> [<s>Śiva</s>] in union there,
